news.title: Trump offers one pc of govt funds recovered through investigations as reward for exposing fraud
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 21 (IANS) US President Donald Trump announced plans to reward people, including journalists, with one per cent of government funds recovered through fraud investigations, as his administration unveiled a broader crackdown involving tougher criminal penalties and the withholding of $1.2 billion in Medicaid payments to California. Speaking in the Oval Office alongside Vice President JD Vance and senior administration officials, Trump said the initiative would encourage Americans to expose suspected corruption and the misuse of taxpayer money. The President said whistleblowers could receive substantial payments for identifying fraud, potentially running into millions of dollars in cases involving large recoveries. "If you turn somebody in and you, let's say, report and you find $1 billion, we are giving a commission to that person of 1 percent," Trump said. He said the proposed incentive would also be available to journalists, subject to applicable laws and approval from their news organisations. "Very few things are more important than good journalism," Trump said, adding that reporters often possessed information that could help uncover wrongdoing. The President said people could report suspected fraud through a new government website, fraud.gov. Trump's announcement went beyond the Justice Department's separately announced Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, which offers payments ranging from $10,000 to $30,000 for qualifying information leading to criminal fraud charges. During the Oval Office interaction, Vance indicated that the administration envisaged a broader reward system linked to recovered money rather than limiting incentives to criminal prosecutions. "Our plan is not to limit this just to criminal prosecutions," Vance said. "It's as the president said, if you find the money and you help us recover it, then you benefit from the program." The administration did not provide a complete written framework establishing how the proposed uncapped one per cent payments would operate alongside existing federal whistleblower laws. Trump also said he would personally resolve disputes over who deserved payments. "I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions," he said. The President said he would make determinations quickly and fairly, potentially dividing awards among competing claimants. Vance, who heads the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, said the initiative emerged from discussions with Trump about involving ordinary Americans in detecting financial wrongdoing. He argued that fraud investigations frequently required coordination among several federal departments and agencies. "Sometimes the fraud will touch seven different departments simultaneously, and you actually need presidential led directive in order to fight that fraud simultaneously," Vance said. Trump claimed that his administration had already uncovered $260 billion in fraud. He also cited investigations involving federal healthcare programmes, food assistance, Social Security and small-business loans. Senior administration officials called for additional legislation imposing mandatory minimum prison sentences for benefits fraud and civil liability on state officials who knowingly failed to prevent fraudulent activities. Those measures remain proposals requiring congressional action. In a separate announcement during the event, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz said the federal government was deferring an additional $1.2 billion in Medicaid payments to California. Oz said the decision concerned personal-care services, whose costs had increased substantially in the state. "We are going to defer $1.2 billion more from California today," he said. He claimed spending on the programme had grown by 24 per cent over three years, approximately twice the average rate elsewhere. Oz said federal officials wanted California to justify the payments before the money was released. The announcement represented a funding deferral, not a final finding that the entire amount involved fraud. Oz also said the administration had deferred approximately $500 million in Minnesota healthcare payments while examining suspected irregularities involving providers. The administration accused Democratic-led states of failing to prevent misuse of public funds. Those political allegations were not accompanied by findings establishing wrongdoing by the state leaders named during the event. The announcement followed the Justice Department's October 20 launch of a whistleblower incentive programme administered by its National Fraud Enforcement Division. news.title: India News | Huge Number of Devotees Participate in Soorasamharam at Tamil Nadu's Kulasekarapattinam Temple
news.text:
Thoothukudi (Tamil Nadu) [India], October 21 (ANI): A huge number of devotees participated in the Soorasamharam, the grand concluding event of the ten-day Dasara festival, at the Sri Mutharamman Temple in Kulasekarapattinam, Thoothukudi district, with devotees describing the occasion as a spiritual experience.

The Soorasamharam, which symbolises Goddess Mutharamman's victory over the demon Soorapadman, is the main attraction of the annual festival and draws large numbers of devotees to the temple.

Also Read | Stocks To Buy or Sell Today, October 21, 2026: Bank of Baroda, TCS and Biocon Among Shares That May Remain in Spotlight on Wednesday.

Devotees attending the event spoke about their longstanding association with the Goddess, their faith and the growing crowds witnessing the celebrations each year.

One of the devotees speaking to ANI recalled his decades-long association with the temple and said he had been making garlands for the Goddess for several years. 

Also Read | Donald Trump Says India-US Trade Deal Is 'Pretty Close', Signals Agreement Soon.

“I am from Mudumuthanmozhi village in Tirunelveli district. I have been making garlands for the Goddess here for the past 35 years. I truly believe that if my health is so good today, it is all because of the Goddess. I have that much devotion towards her. I haven't been making garlands for the past year or two, but I have been doing it since 1991. This is my 36th year visiting the Goddess. It is a wonderful experience. The Goddess is entirely responsible for my good health," said the devotees.

He attributed his good health to his devotion and described the arrangements and the growing participation of devotees at this year's event.

“The Soorasangamam event is going wonderfully today, and everyone is having a devotional and blissful darshan of the Goddess. The arrangements are excellent. The crowd keeps growing year after year. This year, it is even bigger than before. Everything is going really well. People are very happy to see the Goddess.”

Another devotee, Ramanathan, spoke about his nearly four-decade association with the festival, including the years he participated wearing a costume. 

He said, “I have been participating in this festival for almost 40 years. I also wore the costume for about 20 to 25 years. Whatever is meant to happen will happen exactly as it should. When I used to wear the costume, around 40 years ago, we would walk around the temple three times when we set up the stage.”

He recalled the practices followed during the celebrations in the past and expressed happiness at witnessing the Soorasamharam in person after nearly 26 years.

“We would walk around and then step into the fire. But now, whatever the fierce Amman wants to happen will happen. The same applies to people returning home. If people who attend this festival meet with an accident, are involved in a car crash, or suffer a tyre burst on their way home, Amman will bring them home safely. That is why the crowd is so massive. It is a source of immense joy. Today, after almost 26 years, I witnessed the Soorasamharam in person. I am really happy and feel that this is a great victory in my life. Yes, otherwise too,” he added. (ANI)

news.title: Hegseth discusses Iran with Netanyahu in unannounced visit
news.text:
JERUSALEM: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth arrived in Israel on an unannounced visit, and discussed the Iran war with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as tensions continue to simmer between the US and Iran.

Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli PM, confirmed that Netanyahu had met Hegseth at the Uvda air force base in Israel’s southern Negev desert region.

Mr Netanyahu and Mr Hegseth discussed “the threats in the region” and the US-Israel partnership in dealing both “offensively and defensively” with those threats, he said in a brief phone call.

The defence secretary thanked Israel for hosting US forces, which Spielman said numbered in the thousands, and discussed President Donald Trump’s support for the prime minister.

Israeli PM celebrates Trump’s endorsement ahead of next week’s election

“There’s a deep personal relationship here that was at the core of this discussion,” Spielman said.

The Pentagon has not publicly commented on Mr Hegseth’s visit.

Earlier, he posted that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia, but did not specify where he had met the personnel.

Hegseth’s visit comes as tensions flare between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, and Yemen’s Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The Israeli prime minister also said he spoke with President Trump on Sunday about the importance of eliminating the Iranian government.

“We are committed to completing the elimination of the Iranian regime,” Mr Netanyahu said in a statement released by his office. “I have discussed this with Trump many times, including the day before yesterday.”

Netanyahu basks in Trump endorsement

Netanyahu basked in Trump’s endorsement on Monday ahead of close-fought elections, airing a phone call in which the US president predicted he would win, and suggested they may again attack Iran together.

“I think you’re going to have a tremendous victory, actually,” the US president can be heard saying on speakerphone.

“You’re the man I want by my side, Bibi,” Donald Trump said, referring to Mr Netanyahu by his nickname.

Netanyahu, while reminding the famously loose-lipped president that they were on an open line, hailed Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in February.

“Donald, we have a job to finish,” Netanyahu beamed. “We’ll finish it together. We’ll finish it, and no one else will do it.”

Netanyahu did not elaborate, but again described Iran as “the greatest danger”.

Trump, 80, and Netanyahu, who turns 77 on Wednesday, have forged a close partnership at a time when both are vastly unpopular in public opinion in most democratic nations.

The pair have also managed to avoid prosecution while in power, with Mr Netanyahu facing charges of corruption that could land him in prison.

news.title: India, US trade deal to be much different: Trump
news.text:
The US and India are “pretty close” to making a trade deal, which will be much different than the earlier pacts, US President Donald Trump said here.

Speaking to reporters at the Oval Office on Tuesday, Trump said India and the US were pretty close to making a trade deal.

“They want to make a deal. We're going to make a deal. Pretty close, yeah,” Trump said in response to a question.

“It’s going to be a much different kind of deal than we've done," the president said.

Trump’s remarks came at a time Secretary of State Marco Rubio was visiting India and discussed further strengthening bilateral relations focussing on sectors such as trade, energy, technology, defence and people-to-people ties.

Earlier this month, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Milwaukee and Washington to discuss the finer aspects of the trade deal.

India and the US in February announced the finalisation of the framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement (BTA). However, changes in the tariff landscape in the US have led to further negotiations on the pact.

news.title: Meta’s board signals ‘recurring’ failures in oversight of election content
news.text:
PARIS: The oversight board for social media giant Meta said on Tuesday it found “recurrent enforcement failures” in content moderation related to the US midterm elections and Brazil’s presidential election.

The identified failures were often cases of “over-enforcement that suppresses political speech, and under-enforcement that undermines electoral integrity,” said the board, which independently checks moderation on Meta’s Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook platforms.

Social media is a go-to source of electoral information for many voters, raising fears in several countries that it could swing results in favour of certain interests.

Meta’s oversight board, in a statement, noted “the removal of political activist accounts during protests in the US ahead of the midterm elections” and “technical restrictions that hit the accounts of a presidential candidate in Brazil leading to allegations of electoral interference”.

Global affairs officer Joel Kaplan to leave company after 15 years

It added: “It’s clear that Meta must do more to ensure that its enforcement practices during elections are transparent and consistent, and that political speech is protected rather than stifled.”

Brazil election controversy

Brazil’s top electoral court on Monday gave Meta 24 hours to prove it is treating President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing opponent Flavio Bolsonaro equally.

The order came after Lula’s campaign alleged that Meta was suppressing his online content on Instagram and WhatsApp to boost Bolsonaro ahead of a runoff election round on Sunday.

Meta has denied taking any actions to favour one side in Brazil’s election, but previously said that some of Lula’s campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors not isolated to Brazil.

On Monday, the group run by billionaire Mark Zuckerberg apologised on X over another controversy in the United States.

An Instagram account called “No Kings” — after citizen groups protesting what they saw as unconstitutional power grabs by President Donald Trump — was temporarily deactivated on Saturday.

“We sincerely apologise,” Meta spokesman Andy Stone said on X, blaming “automated systems” for taking down accounts that had “very high frequencies” of posts, shares or comments.

Meta’s oversight board reiterated a call for the company to fulfil its promises to make fewer moderation mistakes around elections and political debate.

Joel Kaplan to leave company

Meta Platforms’ chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan will leave the company next year after 15 years there, a spokesperson said on Tuesday.

President and Vice Chairman Dina Powell McCormick will add external affairs to her portfolio, the spokesperson said.

The move comes ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections. McCormick was part of the Donald Trump administration during his first stint as US president. Kaplan was elevated to Meta’s top policy role in January last year, as the social media giant rolled back US fact-checking, ended diversity initiatives and sought closer ties with Trump. A longtime Republican strategist, Kaplan served as deputy chief of staff for policy in the administration of George W. Bush. Meta is among the tech companies facing questions over AI’s impacts, as concerns mount over safety and the industry’s growing footprint among local communities. Trump recently said tech executives, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, had agreed to establish voluntary AI standards.

news.title: World News | French Govt Extends Curfews Amid Nationwide Protests over Rising Living Costs
news.text:
Paris [France], October 21 (ANI): Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised a "massive" police deployment ahead of fresh demonstrations scheduled for October 24. The French government is also extending the curfews and tightening security following days of violent unrest linked to nationwide protests over rising living costs and deteriorating school conditions.

According to CBS News, the announcement followed an admission by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez that authorities had underestimated the unrest and lost control in some cities during Saturday's demonstrations.

Also Read | Strait of Hormuz Tensions Escalate as Iran Says Naval Mines Set Two Oil Tankers Ablaze.

More than 2,500 people had been taken into police custody by Monday evening, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said. The violence included the burning of a historic town hall in Limoges and widespread looting and damage to businesses.

Overnight curfews have been imposed around Paris' Place de la République and the Les Halles shopping district, with similar restrictions introduced in Lyon and other cities. Authorities decided to extend the measures after Paris and Lyon reported no major incidents on Monday night.

Also Read | Donald Trump Says India-US Trade Deal Is 'Pretty Close', Signals Agreement Soon.

President Emmanuel Macron, in an address on Sunday, distinguished peaceful demonstrators from those involved in rioting and looting. He said the government would listen to protesters' concerns while ensuring that those responsible for violence faced legal consequences.

The protests began in mid-September when high school students and teachers in Paris' suburbs demanded action on overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating school buildings and teacher shortages. The movement has since expanded to include trade unions and Yellow Vest activists, broadening into a nationwide campaign against rising living costs and declining public services.

The government has announced plans to deploy more than 3,000 substitute teachers to schools most in need and authorised several hundred additional hires. However, financial pressures and political divisions have complicated efforts to introduce wider reforms.

France's public debt stood at nearly 3.6 trillion euros at the end of June, equivalent to 119 per cent of its annual economic output, CBS News reported. The government expects the fiscal deficit to reach 5.4 per cent of economic output this year and aims to reduce it to 5 per cent in 2027.

Macron's allies also lack a majority in parliament, making it difficult to secure support for major policy measures. (ANI)

news.title: Strait of Hormuz Tensions Escalate as Iran Says Naval Mines Set Two Oil Tankers Ablaze
news.text:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said two oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through routes Tehran considers unauthorised. The announcement, made on Tuesday, October 20, comes amid escalating tensions over control of the strategic waterway, a critical route for global oil shipments.

According to a statement published by the IRGC’s official news outlet, Sepah News, the vessels struck mines laid by Iranian naval forces while attempting to pass through what Tehran described as an illegal crossing point south of the strait. The IRGC said both tankers were set ablaze and brought to a halt. The Iranian military did not identify the vessels or specify when the incidents occurred. Details about casualties, the extent of the damage and the ships’ cargoes were not immediately available in the reports. IRGC Says Oil Tankers Used Unauthorised Route

The IRGC accused the two vessels of attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through a southern route that Iran considers prohibited. It warned that ships using the mined passage would face serious consequences. Iranian forces have increasingly sought to control maritime traffic through the strait, demanding that vessels obtain authorisation before transiting the waterway. Tehran has also warned ships against switching off their navigation and identification systems while operating in the region.

The latest announcement does not independently establish the circumstances surrounding the incidents. The IRGC’s account of the alleged violations and the cause of the fires could not be independently verified in the available reporting.

Iran Also Claims It Shot Down US MQ-9 Reaper Drone

In a separate development, the IRGC said its air defence forces had shot down a US MQ-9 Reaper drone over the Strait of Hormuz on Monday night. According to the Iranian military, its forces were monitoring the region when the drone was detected and destroyed. The claim adds to tensions between Tehran and Washington over military operations and maritime security in the Gulf. The drone incident had not been independently confirmed in the available reports. Iran’s Air Defence Capabilities Surpass Pre-war Levels, Says Army Spokesman Brigadier General Akrami-Nia Amid US Strike Threats.

Strait of Hormuz Tensions Threaten Global Oil Supplies

The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and is one of the world's most important energy shipping routes. Before the current conflict, approximately one-fifth of global oil consumption passed through the waterway, making disruptions there a major concern for energy markets. The latest incidents follow a series of attacks on commercial vessels in and around the strait in recent weeks. Iranian forces have repeatedly reported tankers striking naval mines while attempting to use routes Tehran considers unauthorised.

A separate report on Tuesday said a third tanker had exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the strait, according to Iran's Revolutionary Guards. The vessel was reportedly carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil, although the claims have not been independently verified. The growing risks to shipping have also affected energy markets. Oil prices rose in early trading on Wednesday as traders assessed the threat of further disruptions to crude supplies from the Middle East.

US-Iran Standoff Adds to Maritime Security Concerns

The incidents come amid a wider confrontation between Iran and the United States over the security and control of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has sought to restrict maritime traffic through the waterway, while Washington has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

The situation has increased uncertainty for shipping companies and energy traders, with repeated reports of vessel attacks raising concerns about the safety of commercial navigation.

Further details about the two tankers, possible casualties and the extent of the damage remain unclear. Independent confirmation of the Iranian military's claims was not available at the time of publication.

news.title: Business News | SpaceX Revenue Surges 161% to USD 14.6 Billion in Q3 on SI, Starlink Growth
news.text:
Washington [US], October 21 (ANI): Elon Musk-led aerospace giant SpaceX reported a 161 per cent year-on-year jump in revenue to USD 14.6 billion in the July-September quarter, driven by strong growth in its Super Intelligence business and Starlink connectivity services, as the aerospace company swung to a net profit.

According to the company's third-quarter results, revenue rose from USD 5.6 billion in the same period last year. Net income stood at USD 4.4 billion, compared with a net loss of USD 1.1 billion a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating performance, increased 306 per cent to USD 8.8 billion from USD 2.2 billion.

Also Read | Stocks To Buy or Sell Today, October 21, 2026: Bank of Baroda, TCS and Biocon Among Shares That May Remain in Spotlight on Wednesday.

The Super Intelligence (SI) segment, which includes computing infrastructure, models and software applications, was the biggest contributor to quarterly revenue growth. Its revenue surged 830 per cent year-on-year to USD 7.6 billion, compared with USD 813 million a year earlier.

SpaceX attributed the increase to new cloud services agreements, its acquisition of Cursor and greater adoption of its Grok products among enterprise customers and consumers. The company said it added USD 6.7 billion in year-on-year revenue from SI solutions and infrastructure.

Also Read | Donald Trump Says India-US Trade Deal Is 'Pretty Close', Signals Agreement Soon.

The Connectivity segment, led by Starlink, recorded revenue of USD 5.2 billion, up 69 per cent from USD 3.1 billion a year earlier. Its operating income rose 99 per cent to USD 2.4 billion.

Starlink had 13.6 million consumer subscribers as of September 30, compared with 7.2 million a year earlier. The company added 1.6 million subscribers during the quarter, while monthly average revenue per user increased to USD 69 from USD 66 in the previous quarter.

Space-related revenue rose 6 per cent year-on-year to USD 1.8 billion. SpaceX completed 12 customer launches during the quarter and said its first orbital Starship flight delivered 26 Starlink V3 satellites, adding around 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch.

The results also reflect a sharp increase in investment. Capital expenditure reached USD 19.6 billion during the quarter, compared with USD 6.9 billion a year earlier, largely reflecting spending on computing infrastructure.

SpaceX CFO said the company was focused on expanding its business while maintaining financial discipline. "We are building the infrastructure of the future with discipline--focused on capital efficiency, strong returns on invested capital, and maintaining a robust, investment-grade balance sheet--while moving with the velocity to capture the opportunity in front of us," the CFO said.

SpaceX said computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts as of September 30, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier, as it continued expanding infrastructure to support its Super Intelligence business. (ANI)

news.title: Indian stock markets likely to open marginally positive on global cues
news.text:
A day after a break, domestic markets are likely to open on a positive note on Wednesday amid positive global cues. The sentiment turned positive after the US President Donald Trump said India and the United States are close to finalising a trade deal after more than a year of negotiations.

Gift Nifty at 23,012 signals a flat to positive opening.

All eyes on earnings

The focus will be on Q2 results to be announced by companies. So far, the performance has been mixed. While IT and other sectors have performed well, private banks have posted a weaker-than-expected numbers.

Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, said optimism surrounding a potential India–US trade deal could offer some support to domestic equities, but a sustained recovery may prove difficult as elevated crude oil prices, rising global bond yields and persistent geopolitical uncertainty weigh on investor sentiment. WTI crude is trading around $98–99 a barrel, while Brent is hovering near $110, keeping macroeconomic risks firmly in focus.

“Developments involving Iran and the Strait of Hormuz remain a key source of uncertainty for global markets. Any escalation in tensions could disrupt energy supplies and drive oil prices higher, while signs of meaningful de-escalation may ease pressure on risk assets. Until there is greater clarity on the geopolitical front, investors are likely to remain cautious.

On the domestic front, the September-quarter earnings season is expected to drive stock-specific movements, with investors scrutinising revenue growth, margins and management guidance for signs of resilience amid rising input costs. Foreign institutional investor flows will also be closely watched for indications of whether the recent recovery has the backing of sustained overseas buying,” he said.

Asian equities are offering a more positive lead, buoyed by renewed interest in artificial intelligence-related stocks. Japan’s Nikkei 225 has advanced nearly 1.5 per cent, while South Korea’s KOSPI jumped about 4.7. “However, the strength in regional markets may translate into only limited gains for Indian equities, with elevated oil prices and geopolitical risks likely to temper risk appetite,” said Ponmudi.

Technically also markets remain weak, said analysts.

Pabitro Mukherjee, Deputy Vice President-Research, Bajaj Broking, said the index on Monday’s session formed a sizable bearish candle erasing the previous session’s gains. Overnight, stocks on Wall Street were mildly positive, pushing the S&P 500 0.3% higher as oil prices and Treasury ​yields eased. With 13% of S&P 500 companies reporting, 86% have beaten earnings estimates, according to LSEG data.

“Global ⁠equities were mixed, with solid earnings supporting US markets while ongoing concerns around the AI trade and elevated oil and borrowing costs weighed ​more heavily elsewhere,” Westpac analysts wrote in a note.

“Oil prices fell on unconfirmed reports of renewed peace negotiations, before largely retracing the move ​after the reports were denied.”

news.title: Over three million migrants left US since Trump’s return
news.text:
Washington, Oct 21 (SocialNews.XYZ) The Trump administration said that more than three million migrants have left the United States since President Donald Trump returned to office, as the White House unveiled a sweeping assessment of its immigration crackdown, including a sharp decline in border crossings, mass deportations and tighter restrictions on legal immigration.

In a statement titled "How President Trump Ended the Border Invasion and Restored American Sovereignty", the White House claimed that the population of immigrants living illegally in the country had fallen by at least 2.3 million, describing it as the largest sustained reduction in modern American history.

The administration said nearly 1.2 million people had been deported or removed, while immigration authorities had carried out approximately 1.3 million arrests.

The figures were presented as part of the administration's assessment of its immigration policies and were not accompanied by a comprehensive independent audit.

According to the White House, illegal crossings at the southern border fell by 95 per cent from levels recorded during the Biden administration.

It said nationwide immigration encounters dropped below 380,000 during fiscal year 2026, compared with approximately 2.7 million annually under Biden.

The administration also claimed that no migrants apprehended by the Border Patrol were released into the United States during the fiscal year, describing it as an unprecedented enforcement outcome.

The White House said the immigration court backlog had fallen from more than 4.18 million cases to fewer than 3.09 million.

The reduction followed changes in immigration court procedures, enforcement policies and the handling of pending cases.

However, a decline in the backlog does not necessarily indicate that all affected cases were resolved through final decisions on their merits.

The statement also highlighted a sharp fall in asylum approvals, saying the approval rate had declined to approximately seven per cent from more than 50 per cent during the previous administration.

The White House attributed the change to tougher eligibility assessments and enforcement measures.

Turning to legal immigration, the administration said it had revoked more than 300,000 visas since Trump returned to office.

The revocations included thousands of student visas and visas linked to suspected misuse of immigration programmes, according to the statement.

The administration also cited new restrictions on H-1B employment visas, a category widely used by Indian technology professionals.

It said a $100,000 payment requirement had been introduced for certain H-1B petitions, while the previous random selection system had been replaced with a process intended to favour higher-skilled and better-paid workers.

The White House claimed that H-1B registrations for fiscal year 2027 had declined by 38 per cent under the revised system.

The administration also highlighted the termination of automatic extensions for certain employment authorisation documents and tighter requirements for foreign students and exchange visitors.

It said new screening procedures required greater disclosure of applicants' educational, financial and immigration information.

The White House also pointed to restrictions on immigrant access to federal benefits, including certain healthcare programmes, business loans and government-backed mortgage financing.

It said immigration enforcement agencies had expanded detention capacity, increased deportation flights and strengthened cooperation with state and local authorities.

The administration further claimed that its border policies had contributed to reduced drug trafficking and fewer deaths associated with illegal crossings.

US immigration policy encompasses separate legal pathways for employment, family reunification, education, asylum and permanent residence.

news.title: Donald Trump Says India-US Trade Deal Is ‘Pretty Close’, Signals Agreement Soon
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has said India wants a trade deal with the United States, as both countries continue efforts to finalise a long-pending bilateral trade agreement. The latest development comes amid renewed diplomatic engagement between New Delhi and Washington, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressing optimism that the remaining issues could be resolved soon.

Trump’s Remarks Come Amid Renewed Trade Negotiations

Trump’s remarks come at a crucial stage in negotiations over a proposed India-US trade agreement, which has faced delays amid disagreements over tariffs, market access and other economic issues. The two countries have been working towards an agreement aimed at expanding bilateral trade and improving access for businesses in each other's markets. However, differences over sensitive sectors and the terms of the deal have complicated efforts to reach a final understanding. Discussed Energy Security and Defence Cooperation: Marco Rubio After Meeting EAM Dr S Jaishankar.

While Trump’s statement signals continued interest in an agreement, the deal should not be considered finalised until both governments formally announce its completion.

Marco Rubio Says India-US Trade Deal Is Close

The latest comments follow talks between Rubio and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai on Tuesday, October 20. Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Rubio said Washington and New Delhi were very close to concluding the agreement, adding that only a small number of issues remained to be resolved. He expressed hope that the two sides could wrap up the outstanding matters shortly.

The discussions covered trade, energy security, technology, defence cooperation and regional developments. Both sides reiterated their commitment to strengthening the broader strategic partnership alongside efforts to conclude the trade negotiations. Rubio’s comments followed earlier assurances from US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor and Indian officials that negotiations were progressing, although the final legal language and remaining differences still needed to be addressed. India-US Trade Deal Nears Finish Line, Only 1-2% Issues Left to Resolve: US Official.

What Is Holding Up the India-US Trade Deal?

Despite the positive signals, some differences remain over the terms of the proposed agreement. Market access, tariff treatment and protection for sensitive domestic sectors are among the issues shaping the negotiations. India is seeking favourable tariff rates and stable access to the US market, particularly for its exporters competing with manufacturers in countries such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia. New Delhi also needs to balance US demands for greater market access with the interests of Indian farmers and domestic industries.

The agreement is also being negotiated against the backdrop of tensions over India's purchases of Russian oil and Washington's tariff policy. These issues have complicated bilateral economic ties over the past year.

India-US Trade Deal: What Happens Next?

India's Trade Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on October 15 that the first phase of the trade agreement had been finalised and was undergoing legal drafting. He also said India was seeking preferential market access and greater tariff stability.

Rubio's latest remarks and Trump's comments suggest that both governments remain optimistic about reaching an agreement. However, the final terms, signing date and implementation timeline have yet to be formally confirmed. A completed agreement could provide greater clarity for exporters and businesses in both countries, but its impact will depend on the final tariff arrangements, market-access provisions and protections agreed upon by the two sides.

news.title: I Know What Trump Will Do After Crushing Defeat: Author
news.text:
President Donald Trump will not go gently if the midterms end in a disaster for Republicans as expected, his longtime biographer says.

Author Michael Wolff tells the Inside Trump’s Head podcast that Trump, 80, will react to a midterm defeat as he did after the 2020 presidential election, which eventually snowballed into the Jan. 6 Capitol riot.

“He will understand that what he has to do on the day after,” Wolff said. “The imperative for him is to seize as much attention as he can.”

Wolff recounted how Trump “started his acting out” after Joe Biden was found to have won the election, which included falsely declaring himself the winner on social media and pressuring his Justice Department to overturn the election results.

With only two weeks until Nov. 3, and many polls indicating a blue wave is increasingly likely, both the House and Senate are at risk of coming under Democratic control. Such a development would likely lead to the president’s third impeachment, which the Senate could confirm this time.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Wolff said he does not think Trump’s next possible meltdown will lead to real violence, like on Jan. 6, but the essence of Trump’s rage will manifest similarly in terms of desperate attention-seeking.

“The Democrats, if they win, will be obviously celebrating,” Wolff said. “Obviously trying to impress upon the world that it is a new day. Donald Trump, for his part, will be trying to impress upon the world that he still controls the stage, that it doesn’t make any difference.”

“They may say they won, and they may act like they’ve... won, and maybe they technically have won, but the reality is it is still Donald Trump’s world, and he will do everything possible to make that case,” Wolff said. “And he will do everything possible to make that case the day after and then the day after that.”

Wolff said that after such a defeat, the president may be emboldened to follow through on some of the bonkers threats he has teased this term—such as an invasion of Cuba.

“There will be a series of Trumpian things greater than, you know, greater than anything we’ve ever seen, greater than anything, actually, I think we’ve imagined,” he explained. “Donald Trump will not go willingly. He will not be humbled.”

“That goes back to this idea that he never loses. The idea of humility does not exist in Donald Trump’s soul,” Wolff concluded. “Therefore, he will do the opposite—not retreat, but attack.”

New episodes of incomparable insight into the psyche of the world’s most talked-about man drop every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday evening on YouTube and Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday mornings on other podcast platforms.

news.title: Trump says Iran war could end soon
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 21 (IANS) US President Donald Trump said that the war with Iran could end soon, predicting a sharp fall in global oil prices once the conflict concludes, even as he warned that Washington must ensure Tehran cannot rebuild its nuclear weapons capabilities in the coming years. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office alongside Vice President JD Vance, Trump defended the economic costs of the military campaign, saying higher petrol prices were a relatively small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. The President also criticised European allies for declining to assist the United States during the conflict. Responding to a question about public dissatisfaction with the economy, Trump said the Iran conflict was the principal factor keeping energy prices elevated. "As soon as the war is over, it's going to end very soon the Iran war," Trump said. "Oil is going to drop like a rock and that's the only thing holding it back," he added. The President did not provide a timetable for ending the conflict or explain what military or diplomatic developments could lead to its conclusion. His prediction about oil prices was not supported by a detailed assessment of global supply conditions. The remarks carry particular significance for energy-importing economies, including India, which are vulnerable to fluctuations in international crude prices and disruptions to shipping through the Persian Gulf. Trump defended the administration's military campaign against Iran, arguing that Washington had no alternative because of the threat posed by Tehran's nuclear programme. "You can't let them have it," he said, referring to nuclear weapons. He described Iran as the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism. The President acknowledged public concern about higher fuel prices but said the economic burden was justified. "It's a big price, but actually it's a small price to pay for not letting Iran have a nuclear weapon," Trump said. He claimed that American military operations had severely damaged Iran's nuclear facilities, including installations buried beneath substantial layers of rock. However, Trump said the administration wanted assurances that Tehran would not be able to restore its capabilities several years later. "We could leave right now, and we would have done a good job, a great job," he said. "But it's not good enough for me. We have to make sure it doesn't happen in five years, six years, ten years." Earlier in the same Oval Office interaction, Trump said the United States was making progress against Iran but had not decided how to conclude the campaign. "We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way?" he said. Trump also disclosed that he had contacted several European leaders to ask whether their countries would help the United States. He said the responses were negative. "But I was testing them. I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask would they like to help us? And they said no," Trump said. The President criticised the refusal, arguing that the United States spent substantial sums supporting European security through NATO. "We spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO and they said, no," he said. He did not identify the leaders contacted, specify the assistance requested or explain whether the discussions concerned military operations, logistics or other forms of support. The comments reflected continuing differences between Washington and European governments over the scope of military involvement in the Middle East. Trump also warned that Europe's internal political and immigration challenges were weakening the continent, although those remarks were made in response to separate questions about unrest in France. The Iran conflict has heightened international concerns about energy security, regional stability and the safety of commercial shipping. The Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, is a major route for oil and gas exports to Asian markets.

news.title: Retired admiral Trump’s 'American delusion' is backing US into a corner
news.text:
President Donald Trump is becoming an authoritarian due to his misuse of America's military, a retired admiral warned on Tuesday — and he added that as a result, "all the power in the world will be irrelevant" to stop other threats to America.

"The war in Iran is far from the first time that U.S. policymakers have failed to appreciate the limits of American power," U.S. Ret. Adm. William H. McRaven, who served in the U.S. Navy from 1977 to 2014, wrote for Foreign Affairs on Tuesday. "But the Trump administration’s use of military force against the Islamic Republic since February 28 offers a particularly glaring example of a mistake that has often characterized American strategy in recent decades. The war was launched without a clear rationale and with a constantly shifting set of objectives — from changing Tehran’s regime and squelching its nuclear ambitions to, more recently, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which wasn’t closed until the war started. The results, not surprisingly, have been bad both for U.S. interests and for the Middle East."

He added, "Still, to focus only on the blunders in Iran is to miss a deeper problem in U.S. foreign policy—one that preceded and will outlast Donald Trump’s presidency. Although the particular missteps in Iran may stem from the shortcomings of this president and the team around him, the overestimation of the potential of military force has been a growing feature of American strategy since at least the end of World War II. A tendency to wish away the limits of power accounted for some of the greatest mistakes of U.S. statecraft during the Cold War, with Vietnam the clearest and most consequential example. Yet despite an apparent commitment to internalizing the lessons of that overreach, this American delusion — our excessive faith in the capacity of military power to achieve victory and thereby fundamentally political ends — has gotten worse rather than better, especially in the past quarter century."

From there, McRaven reviewed in detail the history of recent major American foreign policy endeavor, from blunders like the Vietnam War and second Iraq War to successes like the first Iraq War. He concludes that section with Trump's war against Iran, which he characterizes as more aimless than even its other misguided predecessors.

"If I have learned one important lesson in over four decades of military service, it’s that to defeat the enemy, you must stand on the ground he holds dear and own it," McRaven argued.

He then explained how much of this is due to Trump's leadership style, which prioritizes loyalty over competence and integrity. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has either fired or denied promotions to personnel based on political factors, as well as their race and sex.

"The dangers of personalistic presidential leadership are severely exacerbated by more politicized leadership in the military," McRaven concluded. "Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s ongoing purge of military leadership will undermine the civil-military dynamic for years to come. Trump and Hegseth have forced out senior officers across nearly every service, including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the chief of naval operations, and the army chief of staff. Hegseth has intervened to block career advancement in unprecedented ways, personally removing dozens of officers from promotion lists, often with no explanation (although a disproportionate number seem to have worked for leaders who were viewed as obstacles to Trump’s domestic political goals)."

He also pointed out, "While remaining military leaders will largely stay committed to serving honorably and providing their best advice to civilian leaders in the Pentagon and the White House, this purge is bound to have a chilling effect on the willingness and ability of senior officers to give frank counsel, especially when it comes to the costs and limits of what force can achieve."

Ultimately, when it comes to handling future foreign policy challenges, McRaven argued "we will be limited by moral uncertainty... We will be limited by geography... We will be limited by the will of the enemy... We will be limited by our hesitancy to put troops on the ground... We will be limited by time..."

He then stated, as a warning, "Finally, we will be limited by the quality of our leadership, political and military. Without experienced leaders — leaders who understand the need to establish legitimacy, to build coalitions, to have clear and attainable goals, to commit to the task, to limit the duration of the fight to only what is necessary — all the power in the world will be irrelevant."

McRaven is not the first military expert to question Trump's and Hegseth's handling of the American armed forces. Earlier this week, Trump's own former national security adviser, John Bolton, slammed the president's handling of the Russia-Ukraine war.

"If he and Vladimir Putin are good friends, he thinks US-Russia state-to-state relations are good," John Bolton told Times Radio's Andrew Boulton. "That’s not correct for many reasons. Most importantly, because Vladimir Putin doesn’t see Trump as a friend. He sees him as an easy mark. And every time Trump, in a very needy way, comes to Putin to ask for this diesel deal or something like that, Putin’s more than happy to give it to him and put it in his pocket to call him later."

A former ambassador to Russia told this journalist something similar for Salon in 2019.

"What I do know is that things that the president says serves Russia’s national interest, as defined by Putin," McFaul said at the time. "I want to be very clear about that: as defined by Putin. Other Russians have a different definition of the national interest. When the president, for instance, refuses to acknowledge that we were attacked in 2016, as he’s done repeatedly for years now, that serves Putin’s interest, not America’s national interest."

He added, "When he does so standing next to President Putin at a press conference in Helsinki, and when tossed up what should have been a softball question to say he supports his intelligence community, and he chooses not to, in my view that serves Putin’s interests. That does not serve America’s national interest."

He continued, "That raises the question , 'Why is the president consistently siding with Putin on issues where I think it’s not in America’s national interest?' And I think that deserves further examination."

news.title: Elon Musk Backs SpaceX-Tesla Merger As Rocket Firm Turns Profit
news.text: Elon Musk said Tuesday he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public, driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms. Asked about a possible tie-up on a call with analysts, Musk said he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield," but that a combination would be "a good idea."Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly five percent in after-hours trading following the comments. Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders. He added that he could not take part in their talks because he has a conflict of interest. Musk is chief executive of both companies, and also serves as chairman and chief technology officer of SpaceX. He owned 48.4 percent of SpaceX as of June 30, according to a regulatory filing, and controls more than 82 percent of its voting power through super-voting shares. He holds about 20 percent of Tesla. The committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal and there is no guarantee they will, Musk said, cautioning that it would be overstating it to treat a merger as a certainty. Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle." He said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing. His remarks came after SpaceX posted net income of $4.4 billion for the July-September period, compared with a loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier. Revenue jumped 161 percent to $14.6 billion. The quarterly results follow a bumpy start on Wall Street. SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq on June 12 after an IPO priced at $135 a share that raised about $85.7 billion. Its first earnings report as a listed company showed second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion and a net loss of $541 million. The AI division, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," drove the turnaround. Super Intelligence is US President Donald Trump's preferred term for AI.The unit's revenue rose more than nine times from a year earlier to $7.6 billion, overtaking the Starlink satellite internet business as the company's largest source of sales.- Cloud computing -SpaceX credited new cloud services agreements, wider adoption of its Grok chatbot and its acquisition of Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding startup.SpaceX's cloud customers include Anthropic, which agreed in May to pay nearly $45 billion over three years for computing power at SpaceX's Colossus data centers. Google signed on in June, agreeing to pay $920 million a month from October through June 2029.The AI unit turned an operating profit of $431 million, compared with a loss of $1.7 billion a year earlier. As with other AI companies, spending remains heavy. SpaceX invested $19.6 billion in the quarter, $16.4 billion of it in AI, bringing capital spending for the first nine months of the year to $48 billion. Its computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier. Musk said he was "fairly confident" SpaceX could bring an additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity online in 2027. That would come on top of the roughly 2.5 to 3.0 gigawatts it expects to have running by the end of this year.He added that power, cooling and electrical equipment were "somewhat of a limiting factor." Revenue at the Starlink satellite internet unit grew 69 percent to $5.2 billion, and consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million. Average monthly revenue per consumer, however, fell to $69 from $83 a year earlier. Billionaire Ken Griffin said Republican lawmakers and President Donald Trump made a huge blunder by cutting taxes even further last year, reports Bloomberg.

“[W]e didn’t have the fiscal space to renew the tax cuts,” Griffin said in a Tuesday interview at the Future of Global Markets Conference in New York. Griffin was particularly unnerved at U.S. debt eclipsing $40 trillion. And he added that Republicans “have their hands dirty over the tax cuts the last two years, more than spending increases.”

Griffin, a Republican benefactor whose business empire includes hedge fund Citadel and market-maker Citadel Securities, said the solution is to “grow the damn economy,” and to push Europeans to grow theirs, too. 

But he quipped that Trump’s “tariff war with Europe is a fiasco.” 

Despite his criticism of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Bloomberg reports Griffin has been one of “biggest donors this election cycle” of Republicans, even to the point of spending tens of millions of dollars to back the Republican Party’s candidates.

He’s given $10 million to the Senate Leadership Fund and $5 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund. And he also spent “$10 million supporting Byron Donalds,” who’s running for Florida governor. Millions more of his money has gone to backing Republicans in close races, including $2.5 million each for Senators Dan S. Sullivan of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine, reported Bloomberg.

The United States budget deficit, which increased to $1.99 trillion this fiscal year from $1.78 trillion in 2025, “approached its highest level since the pandemic, as spending on the military, safety net programs and interest on the debt dwarfed the Trump administration’s cost cuts, Treasury Department figures showed,” according to New York Times reporter Alan Rappeport.

The ever-widening gap between what the U.S. government spends and what it collects in taxes and other revenue comes at a critical moment when investors are already getting spooked about the nation’s surging debt load. These concerns are coupled with stubborn inflation resulting from Trump’s tariffs and his ongoing attacks on Iran and the subsequent bottleneck of Middle Eastern oil.

All of this is driving up borrowing costs and boosting interest rates for mortgages, credit cards and auto loans, pushing them to their highest levels in two decades earlier this month.

The last time the deficit topped $2 trillion was in 2021, when the pandemic prompted Congress to approve a huge stimulus package to help keep the economy afloat. But analysts point out that there is no pandemic-style crisis forcing the nation to take on that load this time — just a president’s extravagant spending policies.

news.title: Trump offers one pc of govt funds recovered through investigations as reward for exposing fraud
news.text:
Washington, Oct 21 (SocialNews.XYZ) US President Donald Trump announced plans to reward people, including journalists, with one per cent of government funds recovered through fraud investigations, as his administration unveiled a broader crackdown involving tougher criminal penalties and the withholding of $1.2 billion in Medicaid payments to California.

Speaking in the Oval Office alongside Vice President JD Vance and senior administration officials, Trump said the initiative would encourage Americans to expose suspected corruption and the misuse of taxpayer money.

The President said whistleblowers could receive substantial payments for identifying fraud, potentially running into millions of dollars in cases involving large recoveries.

"If you turn somebody in and you, let's say, report and you find $1 billion, we are giving a commission to that person of 1 percent," Trump said.

He said the proposed incentive would also be available to journalists, subject to applicable laws and approval from their news organisations.

"Very few things are more important than good journalism," Trump said, adding that reporters often possessed information that could help uncover wrongdoing.

The President said people could report suspected fraud through a new government website, fraud.gov.

Trump's announcement went beyond the Justice Department's separately announced Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, which offers payments ranging from $10,000 to $30,000 for qualifying information leading to criminal fraud charges.

During the Oval Office interaction, Vance indicated that the administration envisaged a broader reward system linked to recovered money rather than limiting incentives to criminal prosecutions.

"Our plan is not to limit this just to criminal prosecutions," Vance said.

"It's as the president said, if you find the money and you help us recover it, then you benefit from the program."

The administration did not provide a complete written framework establishing how the proposed uncapped one per cent payments would operate alongside existing federal whistleblower laws.

Trump also said he would personally resolve disputes over who deserved payments.

"I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions," he said.

The President said he would make determinations quickly and fairly, potentially dividing awards among competing claimants.

Vance, who heads the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, said the initiative emerged from discussions with Trump about involving ordinary Americans in detecting financial wrongdoing.

He argued that fraud investigations frequently required coordination among several federal departments and agencies.

"Sometimes the fraud will touch seven different departments simultaneously, and you actually need presidential led directive in order to fight that fraud simultaneously," Vance said.

Trump claimed that his administration had already uncovered $260 billion in fraud.

He also cited investigations involving federal healthcare programmes, food assistance, Social Security and small-business loans.

Senior administration officials called for additional legislation imposing mandatory minimum prison sentences for benefits fraud and civil liability on state officials who knowingly failed to prevent fraudulent activities.

Those measures remain proposals requiring congressional action.

In a separate announcement during the event, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz said the federal government was deferring an additional $1.2 billion in Medicaid payments to California.

Oz said the decision concerned personal-care services, whose costs had increased substantially in the state.

"We are going to defer $1.2 billion more from California today," he said.

He claimed spending on the programme had grown by 24 per cent over three years, approximately twice the average rate elsewhere.

Oz said federal officials wanted California to justify the payments before the money was released.

The announcement represented a funding deferral, not a final finding that the entire amount involved fraud.

Oz also said the administration had deferred approximately $500 million in Minnesota healthcare payments while examining suspected irregularities involving providers.

The administration accused Democratic-led states of failing to prevent misuse of public funds. Those political allegations were not accompanied by findings establishing wrongdoing by the state leaders named during the event.

The announcement followed the Justice Department's October 20 launch of a whistleblower incentive programme administered by its National Fraud Enforcement Division. The department said the initiative would provide earlier payments to qualifying informants whose information resulted in criminal charges.

Federal whistleblower programmes have traditionally operated under different statutory and administrative arrangements, including the False Claims Act. The administration's proposed one per cent recovery-based incentive would require clearer implementation rules before its scope, eligibility and relationship with existing programmes could be established.

news.title: US Denies Ordering Starlink Slowdown As Zelenskyy Accuses Musk Of Disrupting Ukraine Network
news.text:
Elon Musk’s SpaceX has come under scrutiny over reported disruptions to Starlink satellite internet services used by Ukrainian forces, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accusing the company of restricting access during the war against Russia.
A report by The Wall Street Journal, citing officials familiar with the matter, said Musk had directed an intentional slowdown of Ukraine’s military Starlink network. The reported move triggered concern in Kyiv and left the Donald Trump administration bewildered, according to the report.
However, senior US officials have denied that Washington ordered any slowdown. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the US military had not directed a reduction in satellite services, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected claims that the White House was responsible for the reported disruption.
US Says It Did Not Order Starlink Slowdown
Speaking to reporters, Hegseth said the US military had not instructed SpaceX to make changes to the satellite internet service used by Ukraine.
“We haven’t pulled anything back,” Hegseth said. “Nothing’s changed from our view. We haven’t made any directives or anything like that. And we wish the Ukrainians obviously success.”
He added that any operational changes or adjustments to the service would fall within the satellite provider’s contractual terms.
“There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied with,” Hegseth said, adding that Starlink had the option to make such decisions.
Rubio Distinguishes Starlink From Military-Grade Starshield
Rubio also rejected allegations that Washington had ordered Starlink’s internet speed to be reduced. He emphasised that Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX, while Starshield is a separate military-grade system used by the US government.
“Starshield is a defence and military product; that is something that the United States military uses. It is not available to Ukraine, and it is under discussion how they want to use it,” Rubio said.
He also questioned Zelenskyy’s understanding of the issue, maintaining that no one in Washington had ordered a slowdown. Rubio said he understood that the reported disruption had been resolved.
“In the United States, nobody ordered that Starlink’s speed be slowed down,” he said, adding that the matter concerned Starlink rather than Starshield, which operates under a contract with the US military.
Rubio said Ukraine was seeking access to Starshield to conduct operations inside Russia but maintained that the reported Starlink disruption had no connection to the White House.
“Ukraine wants access to Starshield… in order to conduct deep strikes inside Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” he said.
Rubio also dismissed claims that Washington had deliberately restricted internet access to prevent certain Ukrainian drones from operating inside Russia.
“No one at the White House ordered the slowdown of the internet so certain drones couldn’t use it,” he added.
Zelenskyy Says Connectivity Disruptions Affected Military Operations
The controversy follows reports of satellite connectivity disruptions that affected Ukrainian military operations as Russian attacks continued.
According to Axios, Zelenskyy raised concerns about the impact of the disruptions on Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.
In an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Piers Morgan Uncensored, Zelenskyy accused Musk of restricting Ukrainian access to Starlink and said the disruption had affected military operations.
The competing accounts have put the spotlight on Starlink’s role in Ukraine’s war effort and the implications of reported connectivity problems for forces relying on the satellite network. While US officials have denied ordering any slowdown, questions remain over the reported disruption and the decisions behind it.

news.title: Justice Kagan warns Supreme Court rulings are fueling polarization and undermining democracy
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday said voting and elections decisions from her conservative Supreme Court colleagues have helped make the country more politically polarized and less democratic.

In a speech two weeks before the pivotal midterm elections for control of Congress, the liberal-leaning justice sharply criticized how the majority’s rulings have affected the nation’s political environment.

“The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effect of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should,” she said during a talk before students and professors at Catholic University’s law school in Washington, D.C.

She blasted rulings that weakened the Voting Rights Act and campaign finance regulations while opening the door for more partisan gerrymandering. She dissented from those decisions. 

“Over the last couple of years especially, both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, … making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” she said. “The people of America look around and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare, and they’re right.” 

The court’s majority, for its part, said in a 2019 ruling that courts drawing voting districts for maximum advantage is a political dispute and federal courts can’t step in. Conservatives have separately ruled that key campaign finance regulations violate the freedom of speech. This year, the court further narrowed protections in the Voting Rights Act, which had helped increase minority representation. 

That helped feed a redistricting frenzy touched off by President Donald Trump, who is trying to hold on to the Republicans’ slim House majorities in the November election. 

Still, Kagan said it’s unfair to say the majority reflexively supports the president. She pointed to key areas where the court has pushed back against Trump, including tariffs, birthright citizenship and mail ballots. 

Lindsay Whitehurst, The Associated Press

news.title: Trump warns Zelensky to make deal with Russia
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 21 (IANS) US President Donald Trump warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that delaying a peace agreement with Russia could leave Ukraine in an increasingly difficult position, arguing that Moscow was steadily gaining territory and that Kyiv might no longer be able to secure the terms available earlier in the conflict. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office alongside Vice President JD Vance, Trump said Russia's military advantage and Ukraine's mounting casualties made a negotiated settlement increasingly urgent. The President also disclosed that he had personally discussed the release of an American prisoner, Stephen Hubbard, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and suggested that there could be developments in the case within days. Trump's remarks came as his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, prepared to travel to Russia following diplomatic discussions in Oslo aimed at advancing efforts to end the war. "Russia's a big machine. They just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done," Trump said. He claimed Russian forces were continuing to capture Ukrainian territory and that the military balance was becoming progressively more difficult for Kyiv. "They've taken a very large piece of land. And, you know, you can say that Ukraine is doing well or poorly, but the land gets bigger and bigger all the time, week by week," he said. Trump's description of battlefield developments was not accompanied by independently verified territorial data. The President argued that Russia's larger population gave it a significant advantage in sustaining a prolonged conflict. He said both countries had suffered enormous casualties but maintained that Ukraine faced greater demographic constraints. "Ukraine has to want to settle this war. Zelensky has to want to settle this war. And if he doesn't, I think it's going to be a very bad thing," Trump said. He argued that Zelensky could have negotiated a more favourable agreement during earlier discussions with Washington. Referring to a previous Oval Office confrontation involving Zelensky, Trump and Vance, the President said the Ukrainian leader had missed an opportunity to secure better terms. "Could have made a good deal then. Could have made a much better deal then probably, possibly, that he can make now," Trump said. The President also criticised the scale of American financial and military assistance to Ukraine, saying Washington had spent hundreds of billions of dollars supporting Kyiv. He claimed the United States had received little in return, although he acknowledged arrangements involving Ukrainian land and rare-earth resources. Trump said European governments were also growing tired of the financial burden of supporting Ukraine. He estimated that Russia and Ukraine had together lost 32,000 people during the previous month, describing most of the casualties as soldiers. The figure was presented as Trump's assessment and was not independently verified. The President said the continuing deaths were among his principal reasons for seeking a settlement. "I thought -- you know, I settled eight wars. I thought that would be the easiest one," he said. Trump attributed the difficulty of reaching an agreement partly to personal hostility between Putin and Zelensky. "The hatred between President Putin and President Zelensky is tremendous. I think that's most of the reason they haven't been able to make a deal, actually," he said. Asked whether the Russian and Ukrainian leaders would have to meet in person to conclude an agreement, Trump said such a meeting was not essential. "They don't have to be in the same room; I guess I can do it another way," he said. He did not explain what alternative diplomatic arrangement he envisaged. In a separate exchange, Trump disclosed that he had raised the case of Stephen Hubbard directly with Putin. "I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard," Trump said. "I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him, let's see what happens," he added. The President declined to confirm whether a prisoner-release agreement was imminent but suggested reporters should revisit the matter within a few days. "I'd love to get him back. It's time to have Mr. Hubbard back," he said. The comments indicated that the administration was pursuing the prisoner's release through direct engagement with Moscow, although no agreement or timetable was announced.

news.title: US offers $30,000 for tips exposing fraud
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 21 (IANS) The United States has launched a $25 million whistleblower programme offering rewards of up to $30,000 to people whose information helps federal prosecutors bring criminal fraud charges, as the Trump administration steps up efforts to detect misuse of taxpayer money. The Justice Department announced the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program (WHIP) on Tuesday, introducing a system under which eligible informants can receive payments much earlier than under traditional federal whistleblower arrangements. The programme will offer awards ranging from $10,000 to $30,000 for original information leading to criminal charges involving specified categories of fraud. The Department of the Treasury has committed $25 million to support the initiative, which will be administered by the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the programme would encourage individuals with knowledge of fraudulent activities to come forward. "Protecting the American people from fraud remains a top priority of the Department of Justice," Blanche said. He said the initiative would allow people to help expose wrongdoing while receiving financial rewards more quickly than under existing programmes. The new system differs from traditional whistleblower arrangements because eligible payments can be made after criminal charges are filed and made public, rather than waiting for a conviction, forfeiture proceedings or the conclusion of appeals. The department said the earlier payment mechanism was intended to encourage prompt disclosure of information and help investigators identify fraudulent schemes before additional public money was lost. Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald, who heads the National Fraud Enforcement Division, said the initiative would expand the government's ability to obtain information about criminal wrongdoing. The department said people submitting information must provide original, specific, truthful and timely evidence that contributes to criminal charges. Participation must be voluntary, and individuals who actively participated in the fraud generally cannot qualify for rewards. A whistleblower may become eligible when the information leads prosecutors to obtain and unseal an indictment or criminal complaint. However, the payment is not automatic. The Justice Department retains discretion to determine whether an individual qualifies and whether an award should be made. The programme also does not require prosecutors to recover a minimum amount of money before considering an early-stage reward. This distinguishes it from other federal whistleblower schemes in which payments may depend on financial penalties or forfeited assets. Individuals who receive an early payment may remain eligible for additional awards under separate government whistleblower programmes if their information subsequently results in substantial financial recoveries. The initiative follows an October 1 directive from McDonald calling for stronger incentives to encourage people to report credible information about fraud. The department said the programme had been developed in 19 days and would initially operate as a three-year pilot. Members of the public can submit information through a federal fraud-reporting portal. The announcement comes as President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have made the detection of fraud involving federal programmes a priority of the administration.
