news.title: US jails Guatemalan man for 30 years over deadly smuggling operation  - Bahamas Spectator – Bahamas &
news.text:
A Guatemalan man has been sentenced to 30 years in a United States prison for his role in a human-smuggling operation that killed 53 migrants trapped in a truck — a disaster that had been described as one of the deadliest such incidents along the US-Mexico border in recent history.

US District Judge Orlando Garcia handed 39-year-old Rigoberto Roman Miranda-Orozco a 30-year prison term on Tuesday, more than a year after his extradition from Guatemala in March 2025.

He was first arrested in Guatemala in August 2024, as part of a cross-border effort to dismantle the human-smuggling network.

The charges stem from a fatal incident on June 27, 2022. According to the US Department of Justice, emergency crews discovered dozens of people trapped inside an abandoned truck in a remote area on the southern outskirts of San Antonio, Texas.

A total of 64 migrants had endured a lengthy journey that began in Guatemala and continued through Mexico across the border into the US.

By the time the truck was driving from Laredo, Texas, to San Antonio — a distance of 250km or 156 miles — prosecutors say the air conditioning had stopped functioning. When the truck was discovered, temperatures were approaching 32 degrees Celsius (90F).

Forty-eight people were pronounced dead on the scene, and five more passed away while receiving emergency medical treatment for heat-related illness and dehydration.

Among the dead were six children and a pregnant woman. Of those killed, 21 were Guatemalan nationals.

Miranda-Orozco has admitted to arranging travel and accommodation for two of the migrants who died in the truck and another who survived but suffered grave injuries.

He pleaded guilty in July to conspiring to bring a migrant into the US resulting in death, as well as aiding and abetting the unlawful entry of migrants resulting in death and serious bodily injury.

According to The Associated Press news agency, Miranda-Orozco is among a group of nearly 20 people sentenced in the US and Guatemala in connection with the tragedy.

Felipe Orduna-Torres, identified as the leader of the operation in the US, was sentenced to life in prison in a federal court in San Antonio in June 2025.

Armando Gonzales-Ortega, described by prosecutors as Orduna Torres’s top assistant, received an 83-year sentence.

Further proceedings remain pending, including in the case against the truck driver.

According to prosecutors, investigators found signs of passengers’ desperate attempts to escape the abandoned truck. Some had reportedly removed clothing. Scratch marks on the trailer’s interior, meanwhile, suggested that some people had clawed at the walls in a futile bid to escape.

The prosecutors said the passengers had paid as much as $15,000 for passage across the border.

“It was clear that they suffered tremendously in their last few hours on this earth,” US Attorney Justin Simmons told reporters at a Tuesday news conference following the sentencing.

The I-35 highway near where the truck was found runs through San Antonio from the Mexican border.

It is considered a popular smuggling corridor because of the large volume of truck traffic, Jack Staton, a former senior official with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), told the Reuters news agency at the time.

The administration of President Donald Trump has cited the need to end human trafficking as a rationale for his crackdown on irregular immigration across the southern border.

But critics have argued that hardline enforcement tactics may drive immigrants to pursue more dangerous methods for crossing the border irregularly.

news.title: Update on Canada's Two Secession Movements
news.text:
Back in June, I wrote a post about Canada's two active secession movements: one in Alberta and one in Quebec. Since then, there have been some important developments. Alberta secessionists suffered a major defeat. Quebec secessionists are in better shape, but the odds are still against them succeeding anytime soon. That said, both movements may well persist for a long time to come.

Yesterday, Alberta secessionists lost a referendum on secession by a massive 75-25 margin. Pollsters expected a blowout, but this margin is close to the outer edge of expectations. Moreover, the result may actually understate the true extent of opposition to secession in the province. As noted in my earlier post, the question put to the voters was not directly about secession, but rather on whether "the Government of Alberta [should] commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada." Essentially, it was a referendum on whether to hold another referendum. Some "yes" voters might have been confused about what it meant or wanted to hold a second referendum, while planning to vote "no."

United Conservative Party Alberta Premier Danielle Smith (who played a key role in arranging yesterday's vote, despite opposing secession herself) has pledged not to hold any further referenda on secession. She may well be happy to sideline an issue that divides her party (Alberta secessionists are overwhelmingly right-of-center UCP voters).

All of this is bleak news for Alberta secessionists. But it's too early to say their movement is dead. As noted in my previous post, secession movements often persist for many years, even in the face of defeats in referenda and other political setbacks. Scotland, Quebec, and Catalonia are all examples of this phenomenon. And some 25% of Alberta voters did express support for secession, despite opposition from the leaders of all major political parties. That's a minority, but far from an insignificant one.

Meanwhile, in Quebec, on October 5, the secessionist Parti Quebecois (PQ) won the provincial election. But they got only 28% of the vote (the lowest percentage for any winning party in the history of Canadian provincial elections). That translated to a "minority" government that has 59 seats in Quebec's National Assembly (the provincial legislature), 5 short of a majority. And, as discussed in my previous post, secession remains unpopular, with polls showing opposition by a margin of 2-1 or more. For much more detailed discussions of the Quebec election and its ramifications, see analyses by Canadian election/polling experts Eric Grenier and Philippe Fournier.

As Fournier emphasizes, PQ leader Paul St. Pierre Plamondon (known as "PSPP") remains committed to holding a secession referendum. But the minority nature of his governments makes it unclear whether the PQ can find the votes to enact legislation to hold one. The left-wing Quebec Solidaire party (which holds 9 seats) is also pro-independence. But they may not be willing to work with the PQ. In addition, PSPP has promised not to hold a referendum so long as Donald Trump remains president of the United States, claiming it would be too dangerous to do so while Trump continues his trade war with Canada and otherwise threatens the country. Unless Trump dies or gets impeached and removed (both relatively unlikely), he will remain in office until January 2029. Canadian minority governments generally don't last more than two years. So PSPP may not be in power long enough to outlast Trump.

While Quebec secessionists seem unlikely to prevail in the near future, the fact that they managed to return to power is still a sign of the movement's persistence. And they have survived referendum defeats in 1980 and 1995. Thus, the movement is likely to continue to be a thorn in the side of Canadian federal governments, perhaps for many years to come. It has demonstrated its staying power over many years, much more so than Alberta secessionists.

Many Canadians believe Trump's threats against their country have weakened secessionists in both Alberta and Quebec. PSPP's stance is just part of the evidence for this conclusion. Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the "51st state" have bolstered national unity and made the Liberal Party government of Prime Minister Mark Carney much more popular than might otherwise be the case. Trump is making Canadian national unity - and the Canadian Liberal Party - great again! But for him, the Liberals would likely have lost last year's Canadian federal election to the Conservatives.

Perhaps, all along, Trump has been trying to help the Liberals and stymie secessionists. If that's the true objective of his Canada policy, then maybe it's not quite as evil and stupid as otherwise seems to be the case. On a more serious note, Trump's policies have illegally usurped congressional authority over trade, damaged our economy, and alienated a crucial ally - all for no good reason.

In my June post, I outlined reasons why I am more sympathetic to Alberta's secession movement (motivated by conservative economic ideology and grievances about federal fiscal transfers and energy policies), than Quebec's (motivated by Francophone ethno-nationalism). Although I think the Alberta movement has greater merit than Quebec's, for reasons also summarized in the earlier post, I remain skeptical that Alberta secession would accomplish more good than harm. I also explained why these movements may be of interest to many non-Canadians and why I (an American) comment on them them:

[T]hese events are… of interest to students of federalism and secession, and to anyone who cares about the future of America's northern neighbor and one of our most important allies. And history shows that secession movements often persist even after defeat in a referendum…. From a US perspective, I worry that a successful secession movement would make Canada a weaker and less effective ally. Unlike our current president, I think a strong Western alliance is essential…. Some might find it inappropriate for an American to comment on Canadian politics. I disagree. Canadians and other non-Americans often express views on US politics. And they have every right to do so. Political analysis should be judged on its substance, not on the background of the author. In addition,… Canadian secessionism potentially impacts the US in various ways, and raises broader issues about the morality of secession movements that Americans and others have reason to take an interest in…. I am a longtime academic expert on federalism and secession-related issues, and I know French, as well as English. Thus, I think have the necessary qualifications to write about these issues. Whether the commentary is any good or not, is for others to judge.
news.summary: Alberta secessionists lost a referendum by a large margin. Quebec secessionists are in better shape, but still facing an uphill struggle.

news.title: 'Race to the bottom': Justice Kagan unleashes on Supreme Court conservatives
news.text:
NBC News reports Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday sharply criticized the Supreme Court’s conservative majority, saying it had undermined democracy with a series of rulings, including several that have prompted a new wave of legislative map-drawing that has increasingly eliminated competitive districts.

“Kagan, who has dissented in those cases, also took aim at the majority for striking down campaign finance restrictions and, as she put it, the ‘evisceration’ of the landmark 1965 Voting Rights Act that was enacted to protect minority voters,” reports NBC News.

“Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions,” Kagan told the Catholic University’s law school in Washington D.C. “I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should.”

Kagan cited the 2019 SCOTUS ruling claiming federal courts could not intervene to limit extreme undemocratic gerrymandering. And she also referenced a series of rulings that gutted the Voting Rights Act, including one this year that led to Republican states eliminating majority Black districts. 

At President Donald Trump’s behest, conservative states redrew their congressional maps to maximize the number of seats the majority party can win in that state, often at the expense of majority Black districts. Texas kicked off the mid-decade redistricting, which forced blue states like California to try to mitigate the dame. This in turn, prompted still more red states to enter the fray in what Kagan called “a race to the bottom.”

The lopsided maps deny people “their rights to voting equality,” she said, and they have the effect of “driving people away from the center, towards the wings, toward the extremes” because candidates only have to worry about winning the primary. She added that the failure of the court to take action on the issue is “making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so.”

In addition, the conservative court majority consistently struck down campaign finance restrictions, which allows parties to flood campaigns with cash.

“I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they’re right,” she said during a question-and-answer session with professor Joel Alicea.

news.text: Washington DC: US President Donald Trump has once again warned that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy must commit to negotiating an end to the war with Moscow, cautioning that a failure to do so will lead to severe consequences.Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump placed the onus directly on Kyiv to seek a resolution to the ongoing conflict."Ukraine has to want to settle this war. Zelenskyy has to want to settle this war," Trump said. "And if he doesn't, I think it's going to be a very bad thing."Expressing frustration with the scale of American financial support sent to Ukraine, Trump argued that US taxpayers have received no return on their investment while continuing to face economic fallout."Look, we have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We've got nothing back other than high diesel," Trump stated. "We have given probably more money to Ukraine than almost anybody over the years, hundreds of billions of dollars. We got nothing back. "Week by week, it just—they march forward. They just keep marching forward. They have an unlimited supply of people, this too."On Monday (local time), Trump expressed willingness to hold a high-stakes trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to end the war in Ukraine and pursue global denuclearisation, even if Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is excluded from the negotiations.Speaking to reporters at the White House before departing for Kansas, Trump confirmed he would readily meet with the Russian and Chinese leaders to broker peace and halt nuclear proliferation."Anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not, whatever I could do to end the war," Trump said when asked if he would meet with Xi and Putin without Zelenskyy present."And they do want to have a meeting. news.title: How Bernie Sanders Could Hurt Talarico and Hinojosa in Texas
news.text: As progressive independent Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont rallied supporters in Houston on Tuesday, two of Texas Democrats' highest-profile candidates were notably absent. Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa did not attend Sanders' Houston stop on his "Fighting Oligarchy" tour, an absence that comes as polling suggests that democratic socialism remains unpopular with most Texas voters. Both candidates are trying to appeal beyond the Democratic base in a state where winning a top office requires support from independents and crossover Republican voters. Political scientists say Sanders' campaign events give Republicans an opportunity to portray Texas Democrats as aligned with the party's left wing. "Any effort by Bernie Sanders is likely to be more of a negative than a positive for Texas Democrats," Rice University political scientist Mark Jones told Newsweek. "They don't really need to worry about enthusiasm. Donald Trump does that all on his own in terms of motivating Democrats to turn out." Newsweek has reached out to the Sanders, Talarico and Hinojosa campaigns for comment. What the Texas Polls Show A June 2026 University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll found democratic socialism was viewed favorably by 29 percent of Texans and unfavorably by 46 percent, leaving the ideology 17 points underwater statewide. Because of that, Jones argued, appearing with Sanders could create more problems than benefits for candidates trying to build broader coalitions. "I believe James Talarico is right. That's a smart thing to do," Jones said of the Senate candidate's decision not to attend Tuesday's rally. "Any Democratic candidate who shows up probably has been poorly advised." University of Houston political scientist Brandon Rottinghaus offered a similar assessment. "Senator Sanders's visit complicates the Democrats' centralized messaging on affordability," Rottinghaus told Newsweek. "His more progressive view gels with that take, but also opens up the doors to other kinds of progressive issues Democrats may not want to use as their closing argument to voters." Rottinghaus said Republicans have spent much of the election cycle attacking what they characterize as Sanders-style socialism. "Texas Republicans have been running against Bernie Sanders-style socialism all cycle and his visit is likely to generate opposition among Republicans as much as support among Democrats," he said. Republicans have already sought to capitalize on Sanders' Texas visit. On Tuesday, Governor Greg Abbott's campaign released a statement titled, "SANDERS' TEXAS VISIT PUTS SPOTLIGHT ON HINOJOSA'S HIGH-TAX RECORD," trying to tie the Democratic gubernatorial nominee to Sanders and the policies Republicans frequently label socialist. Vice President JD Vance flew into Tyler on Tuesday, days after Trump's third trip to Texas in a month. He told the crowd that electing Talarico was the only way to "screw up" the state's future, and said the Democrat takes positions that clash with the moderate image he is now presenting to statewide voters. "James Talarico needs to take a week or two to get his own head examined because he's lost his damn mind," Vance said. What Early Voting Turnout in Texas Shows Both parties see signs of hope in early voting turnout in Texas so far. The state's urban centers, which are Democratic powerhouses, showed record turnout for a midterm, but so did the heavily Republican suburbs. The Harris County Elections Department reported on X that by 3:30 p.m. Monday, more than 70,000 voters had been processed, surpassing the previous record of 63,188 set in 2018, with 3 1/2 hours remaining. Dallas County also broke its record for the first day of early voting of any election. Judge Clay Jenkins reported on X that the county had 76,069 voters Monday, surpassing the previous record of 60,573 voters in 2020. Turnout in El Paso County on the first day of early voting was the second highest on record for a midterm election. Voting records were also set in the GOP stronghold of Denton County, suggesting both sides flocked to the polls Monday to make their voices heard. Texas Democrats Rally for Voter Turnout Former Texas Congressman Beto O'Rourke acknowledged Democrats' long history of disappointment in the state but argued this cycle feels different. "I've been doing this a long time. I, like you, have had my heart broken by Texas more than once," O'Rourke told supporters at the Sanders rally. "But the way that I look at it, it just makes our hearts stronger, beat more powerfully, and in this moment, all of our hearts are coming together at the right time, right when we needed it." Sanders focused less on electoral politics and more on his normal talking points of economic inequality, healthcare and the influence of wealthy donors in American politics. "In the richest country in the history of the world, we should be able to provide a decent standard of living for every man, woman, and child," he said. The self-described democratic socialist received roughly 33 percent of the vote in Texas' 2016 Democratic presidential primary, losing decisively to Hillary Clinton. Four years later, Sanders won about 30 percent of the vote, finishing behind eventual Democratic nominee Joe Biden, who received about 35 percent. What Latest Polls Show in Texas Abbott, who is making a bid to become Texas' longest-serving governor, is ahead in most recent polls by about 3 to 4 percentage points. The RealClearPolitics average of polls on Tuesday, for example, has Abbott ahead by 48.7 percent to Hinojosa's 45.3 percent. The latest CBS News/YouGov poll, conducted among 1,460 likely voters between October 8 and 16, gave Abbott 52 percent to Hinojosa's 48 percent. A University of Houston Hobby School of Public Affairs poll, which surveyed 2,000 likely voters between October 10 and 14, found Abbott ahead by three points, 49 percent to Hinojosa's 46 percent. Talarico has led most recent polls over Paxton by 2 or 3 percentage points. The RealClearPolitics average of polls on Tuesday has Talarico leading by 2.2 points—48.5 percent to Paxton's 46.3 percent. The most recent survey in that average, a CBS News/YouGov poll of 1,458 likely voters conducted from October 8 to 16, had Talarico up 51 percent to 49 percent. Paxton has led in only one of the six most recent public surveys. An InsiderAdvantage poll of 1,200 likely voters between October 13 and 14, showed Paxton with a narrow lead, 49 percent to Talarico’s 48 percent. Most of the leads are inside the margin of error. Early voting started Monday and ends October 30 in Texas. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa did not attend Bernie Sanders' Houston rally.

news.title: Lula campaign seeks to disqualify Bolsonaro over Meta ‘interference’
news.text:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign team will request the disqualification of rival Flavio Bolsonaro on Tuesday over alleged election interference by tech giant Meta, a source told AFP.

Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term in office but is facing stiff competition from his right-wing challenger, the son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro.

Flavio Bolsonaro received 47 percent of the vote over the incumbent’s 45 percent in the first round earlier this month, and polls show a technical tie ahead of Sunday’s runoff.

The petition to be submitted to Brazil’s top electoral court concerns alleged “algorithmic manipulation” by Meta aimed at harming Lula’s chances of winning, the campaign source said.

The information was first revealed Monday by Brazilian newspaper Folha de S. Paulo.

Meta and lawyers from both campaigns will meet at the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) on Tuesday, a court source said.

The court on Monday gave Meta 24 hours to prove it was complying with an order to treat both campaigns equally, threatening a daily fine of around $200,000 if it didn’t.

The order came after Lula’s campaign alleged that Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, was suppressing his online content to boost Bolsonaro.

“We have completed the implementation of the measures to comply with the Superior Electoral Court’s decision,” the company stated on Tuesday.

Lula seeks fightback

Lula’s campaign also alleged inconsistencies in WhatsApp’s artificial intelligence tool, saying Lula-related election content was limited while Bolsonaro content was untouched.

Meta has denied taking any actions to favor one side in the election, but previously said that some of Lula’s campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors.

Dozens of Lula supporters protested outside the company’s Sao Paulo offices on Monday, bearing placards and chanting slogans like “Meta out of Brazil.”

Lula, 80, has also accused the American government of meddling in the elections in favor of Flavio Bolsonaro.

US President Donald Trump has not yet explicitly endorsed Bolsonaro, 45, but called his surprise first-round finish a “very, very big victory.”

The runoff victor will either preserve the vast country of 214 million people as a left-wing stronghold in Latin America, or usher it into the ranks of right-wing administrations loyal to Trump.

The shock result of the first round appears to have invigorated the left, with Lula’s camp staging massive rallies ever since and seeking to up its social media game.

Flavio’s father Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his electoral defeat to Lula in 2022.

Flavio Bolsonaro has sworn to liberate his father if elected.

news.title: Don Jr. opposed Iran war and told his dad not to start one: report
news.text:
Donald Trump Jr. privately urged his father not to launch a military campaign against Iran and has consistently expressed opposition to the conflict, according to a recent report by The Atlantic.

Trump Jr. made his stance clear to President Donald Trump when the operation began and has continued to criticize the war in private settings, two people who spoke with the president’s eldest son told the publication. 

Though he has remained publicly silent to avoid breaking with his father, sources noted that his skepticism toward foreign intervention has long been established.

“Don has kept his views on the subject private, as he would never publicly break with his dad on an issue like this, but I can’t imagine anyone who knows Don would be surprised by his personal views on the subject,” a person close to Trump Jr. told The Atlantic.

The report points to a broader division within the administration and the conservative movement regarding foreign military intervention. Other senior figures, including Vice President JD Vance, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, also expressed initial skepticism or private reservations about joining Israel’s military campaign and its proposed scope.

The conflict faces mounting criticism as its economic and political costs rise. 

Recent polling from the Pew Research Center found that 65 percent of Americans disapproved of the administration’s handling of the Iran operation, while gas price increases linked to energy market disruptions continued to affect household budgets. Prominent party figures have raised concerns over the timeline, with House Speaker Mike Johnson urging the president to end the conflict as far back as July.

The White House did not address Trump Jr.’s reported objections directly, but an official stated that “Iran has been decimated, and one way or the other, the conflict in Iran will be over very soon.” 

Domestic fuel costs have added to the administration’s troubles, with average gas prices remaining above $4 per gallon for a record 158 consecutive days following supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. The price surge drove U.S. inflation to a three-year high of 4.2 percent in May, leaving consumers paying tens of billions more at the pump compared to the previous year. 

The economic strain appears to be weakening Republican standing ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. 

Recent polling from Politico showed that 29 percent of undecided voters would remain unpersuaded to support GOP candidates even if fuel prices dropped by a dollar, while prices in several Western states have climbed to more than $5 and $6 a gallon.

news.title: Trump says Iran war could end soon
news.text:
Washington, Oct 21 (SocialNews.XYZ) US President Donald Trump said that the war with Iran could end soon, predicting a sharp fall in global oil prices once the conflict concludes, even as he warned that Washington must ensure Tehran cannot rebuild its nuclear weapons capabilities in the coming years.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office alongside Vice President JD Vance, Trump defended the economic costs of the military campaign, saying higher petrol prices were a relatively small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.

The President also criticised European allies for declining to assist the United States during the conflict.

Responding to a question about public dissatisfaction with the economy, Trump said the Iran conflict was the principal factor keeping energy prices elevated.

"As soon as the war is over, it's going to end very soon the Iran war," Trump said.

"Oil is going to drop like a rock and that's the only thing holding it back," he added.

The President did not provide a timetable for ending the conflict or explain what military or diplomatic developments could lead to its conclusion.

His prediction about oil prices was not supported by a detailed assessment of global supply conditions.

The remarks carry particular significance for energy-importing economies, including India, which are vulnerable to fluctuations in international crude prices and disruptions to shipping through the Persian Gulf.

Trump defended the administration's military campaign against Iran, arguing that Washington had no alternative because of the threat posed by Tehran's nuclear programme.

"You can't let them have it," he said, referring to nuclear weapons.

He described Iran as the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism.

The President acknowledged public concern about higher fuel prices but said the economic burden was justified.

"It's a big price, but actually it's a small price to pay for not letting Iran have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.

He claimed that American military operations had severely damaged Iran's nuclear facilities, including installations buried beneath substantial layers of rock.

However, Trump said the administration wanted assurances that Tehran would not be able to restore its capabilities several years later.

"We could leave right now, and we would have done a good job, a great job," he said.

"But it's not good enough for me. We have to make sure it doesn't happen in five years, six years, ten years."

Earlier in the same Oval Office interaction, Trump said the United States was making progress against Iran but had not decided how to conclude the campaign.

"We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way?" he said.

Trump also disclosed that he had contacted several European leaders to ask whether their countries would help the United States.

He said the responses were negative.

"But I was testing them. I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask would they like to help us? And they said no," Trump said.

The President criticised the refusal, arguing that the United States spent substantial sums supporting European security through NATO.

"We spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO and they said, no," he said.

He did not identify the leaders contacted, specify the assistance requested or explain whether the discussions concerned military operations, logistics or other forms of support.

The comments reflected continuing differences between Washington and European governments over the scope of military involvement in the Middle East.

Trump also warned that Europe's internal political and immigration challenges were weakening the continent, although those remarks were made in response to separate questions about unrest in France.

The Iran conflict has heightened international concerns about energy security, regional stability and the safety of commercial shipping. The Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, is a major route for oil and gas exports to Asian markets.

news.title: Right-wingers erupt at airline CEO for supporting more taxes on the rich
news.text:
Even as President Donald Trump tries to keep Republicans in control of Congress by offering voters $5,000 if they win, his fellow conservatives are denouncing a business leader for advocating the supposedly socialistic idea of raising taxes on the rich.

"Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a 'danger to society' and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview," reported The Guardian's Gaya Gupta on Tuesday. "Talking to the New York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust."

Kirby said in the controversial statement, “We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100 percent at some level. I would pay them.”

Gupta described the reaction as heated.

"In response, headlines from Fox Business and the New York Post decried that Kirby made $32 [million] in 2025," Gupta wrote. "In response to Kirby’s comments, Glenn Beck, a former Fox News host, and other users on X called for a boycott of United Airlines. Jeff Landry, Louisiana’s governor, said the statement was 'audacious.'"

Landy wrote on X, “How audacious from a guy that didn’t even build @united and makes $32 million a year.” After suggesting that Kirby donate to the government, he said, "better yet, he should distribute his salary to the employees at the bottom of the ladder @united!”

He concluded, “Let’s see you step up and place your money where your mouth is!”

These reactions are consistent with the Trump era emphasis on opposing anyone who advocates wealth redistribution, characterizing such policies as inherently socialistic. In the process, Trump and his supporters harken back to political methods that succeeded for the Republican Party in the 1950s and 1980s.

"These are not mere political disagreements, like differences over taxes or regulations," Trump said in a July speech. "Communism is a mortal threat to American liberty. … The godless communist morality states that anything is justified to bring about inhuman visions. … They don’t want good, they don’t love God, and they don’t want God."

Despite this rhetoric, Trump has been accused by fellow conservatives as well as non-conservatives of supporting socialistic policies despite saying he opposes socialism. This includes his proposed $5,000 giveaway to every American adult if Republicans reclaim Congress, his stakes and shares in businesses that work with the government and his use of tariffs to help loyalists at the expense of those without connections to the state.

Minutes into his rally in Greenville Tuesday night, Trump was heckled by two protesters in succession. 

“They get home, and they get smacked in the face by the mother and the father, maybe a little harder by the father. And they say, ‘We voted for that man. We love that man. You did that — how disgraceful,’” Trump said, using the same jab he’s hit protesters with at rallies in Texas, Ohio and Alaska this month.

But then he took it a step further — likening the demonstrators interrupting his speech to the thousands of people who have been arrested for rioting and looting during ongoing protests in France against the rising cost of living and poor conditions in schools. 

As Trump travels across the country to campaign for Republican candidates ahead of November’s midterm elections, he has struggled to get through a speech without getting interrupted by protesters. 

“They get paid by the radical left lunatics that you watch taking place in France,” Trump said. “I would say this is a slightly lesser event,” he then admitted. 

French President Emmanuel Macron blamed the violence in France on “seditionists from far-left fringe groups, joined by many criminals,” during his national address Sunday. 

During another disruption later that night, Trump said, “Don’t hurt them,” but then mimicked wanting to punch them — a callback to his first presidential campaign in 2016 when he encouraged his supporters in Iowa to “knock the crap out of” anyone preparing to throw tomatoes.

Trump was in Greenville Tuesday night to stump for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, whom he called “fantastic.” The president mentioned Whatley’s time as chair of the Republican National Committee with his daughter-in-law Lara Trump during the 2024 election cycle. 

He went on a bizarre tangent about Lara’s body, telling the crowd, “She’s an extremely fit young woman. Have you ever seen her exercise?” 

“She’s so fit it’s ridiculous,” he added. “But she’s also fit up here,” Trump said while pointing to his head. “The two of them were unbelievable.”

Whatley was trailing the state’s former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper by more than 10 points in a recent poll. Fifty-two percent of voters in North Carolina said they’d vote for Cooper, compared to 39 percent who backed Whatley, according to the Elon University/YouGov survey. 

Trump is known for commenting on the looks of people at his rallies, specifically women. But he recently made headlines for gushing over Republican Sen. Jon Husted’s butt at an Ohio rally last week.

“I’m studying his body. I’ve never studied the body of a man before. It’s not my thing,” Trump said Tuesday night as he recalled checking out the former college football star in Ohio. “But I looked at his a**.” 

The president then likened Husted’s butt to “a pile of muscle.”

Trump has been fiercely campaigning for GOP candidates in red states, where Republicans would normally win easily. But the party in power typically loses seats in the midterms, and Democrats are gaining ground in several of these states, such as Texas and Kansas.

As Trump spends his nights trying to boost Republicans’ chances in their races, telling his supporters to pretend that he’s on the ballot, the president is dealing with his own record-low approval ratings. 

Just 33 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s job as president, while 66 percent disapprove, according to a recent Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll. 

The Trump administration has been dogged by an unpopular Iran war, stubborn inflation, and an immigration crackdown that critics believe is too aggressive.

news.title: Democratic PAC Puts $1.2 Million Into Mississippi Senate Race
news.text:
The Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC (SMP) is spending $1.2 million on advertisements through Nov. 3 to boost Democrat Scott Colom in the Mississippi U.S. Senate race.

The investment shows Democrats think they can win in Mississippi, a state no Democratic presidential candidate has carried since Jimmy Carter won it in 1976.

Colom will face Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Nov. 3 general election.

“SMP is going up on TV in Mississippi. $1.2 million behind Scott Colom, starting tomorrow and running through Election Day,” SMP spokeswoman Lauren French said Tuesday in a post on X. “This is the first time SMP has spent in this race. It won’t be the last thing you hear about it.”

French said Colom is running a competitive race, and Cindy Hyde-Smith is “on her heels.”

Hyde-Smith responded to the investment by the Democratic PAC.

“Scott Colom and his out-of-state billionaire donors want to open our borders, raise your taxes, and move our nation closer to socialism,” Hyde-Smith said in a post on X on Tuesday. “Make your voting plan now!”

The Hyde-Smith campaign pointed out how long it took for the Democrats to spend money supporting Colom’s campaign.

“It took Chuck Schumer and his Super PACs 13 months to run a single ad for Scott Colom,” Nathan Calvert, communications director for the Hyde-Smith campaign, said in an email to The Epoch Times. “Chuck knows what Mississippians know, Scott Colom is too liberal, he supports transgender surgeries for children, men in women’s restrooms and locker rooms, open borders, and higher taxes. Team Cindy is confident that voters will reject this radical agenda at the ballot box on Nov. 3.”

The Democrats have talked about spending money in Mississippi and believed early in 2025 that they could compete in the state, French said on X.

“None of this came out of nowhere. Democrats have talked about Mississippi all cycle,” French said. “Most notably Leader Schumer, who has made the case since the early days of 2025 that Democrats can and should compete in Mississippi.”

The Colom campaign didn’t respond to an email seeking comment.

President Donald Trump gave Hyde-Smith his endorsement in March 2025.

“Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith is 100% MAGA, and doing a fantastic job representing the Incredible People of Mississippi!” Trump said in a 2025 post on Truth Social. “An Original Member of my Mississippi Leadership Team, Cindy has been with us from the very beginning. In the Senate, Cindy is fighting hard to Secure our Border, Grow the Economy, Champion our Amazing Farmers and American Agriculture, Support our Brave Military/Veterans, Promote Energy DOMINANCE, and Defend our always under siege Second Amendment.”

Colom’s endorsements include several unions, mayors in Mississippi, and U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.)

The Republicans hold a majority in the U.S. Senate. There are 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and two independents, Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine, who both caucus with the Democrats.
news.summary: Fight for control of the U.S. Senate is attracting money in Mississippi.

news.title: Vivek Ramaswamy’s Election Odds Crash to New Low Amid Amy Acton Ad Backlash
news.text: Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy's odds on prediction markets crashed Tuesday amid backlash to a widely circulated video involving the long-estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent. Prediction market site Kalshi posted to X on Tuesday, saying that Acton hit a new high with a 76 percent chance of winning the governor's mansion. As of 4 p.m. ET, Ramaswamy's odds sunk to 26.8 percent, a new low on the site. Polymarket similarly posted on Tuesday that Ramaswamy's odds crashed to a new low of 30 percent. As of 4:19 p.m. ET, the Republican's odds dipped further on the site to 22 percent. The prediction market lows come on the heels of a video clip shared on X, including by journalist and podcast host Walter Curt's account. "My name is Donna Arthur, and I’m Amy Acton’s mother," the speaker says at the start of the video. She continued, saying, "I love my daughter" but accused her of lying about her opponent and upbringing, saying, "Amy has a serious problem; she is a liar." The woman said that Amy "has lied her entire life," adding that she needs help. "Don’t let her become your governor," the speaker later adds. The video posted to Curt's X account has been seen over 5 million times and reposted over 9,000 times. The statements by Acton’s mother in the video clip are allegations, not independently established facts, while published accounts describe Acton’s childhood as unsettled. The Democratic gubernatorial candidate told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio, in part that she "was removed from [her birth mother] at the age of 12," the Associated Press reported. Her parents divorced when she was 3 years old, and she lived in around 18 homes by age 12 while moving frequently with her mom and spent one winter in a tent at a campground, local outlet WKBN27 reported. The video clip of Acton’s mom does not explicitly explain when the video was made or who financed its production. While speaking to reporters Tuesday night, Ramaswamy took credit for the ad, saying, "It is an ad from our campaign." "The thing that I want to say is that I would love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans, and unfortunately Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues, she won't debate me," he added. In a sharply worded statement provided to Newsweek earlier Tuesday by Acton’s campaign, Philip Stearns accused Ramaswamy of exploiting his sister’s account of childhood sexual abuse for political purposes and condemned the video as a personal attack. Newsweek has reached out to Ramaswamy's campaign via email on Tuesday for comment regarding the backlash and new lows in prediction markets. Backlash Pours in as Ramaswamy's Campaign Responds As the video circulated social media on Tuesday, people vocalized their opposition to the ad. “We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor," Connie Luck, spokesperson for the Ramaswamy campaign, told Newsweek in an emailed statement earlier Tuesday. “Ohioans are struggling with rising costs and need a governor who can help them. Vivek wants the election to focus on how to solve these problems, but unfortunately Amy Acton has repeatedly resorted to lying about Vivek and his family, lying about her own record, and then hiding from debates and hiding from voters by barring cameras at her own events. “Vivek has accepted debate invitations from CNN and WLWT because he believes Ohioans deserve to hear directly from the people asking to lead their state. He stands ready to defend his record against Amy Acton’s defamatory lies. If Amy disagrees with these criticisms, she should stand before the people of Ohio, answer the questions, and let voters decide for themselves. The fact that she won’t, and Vivek will, should tell you everything about who’s really lying.” Meghan McCain, conservative commentator and daughter of late Arizona Senator John McCain, called the video "dastardly." "This is a dastardly ad. It never should have been created. Shame on whatever consultant firm created this," McCain said. Lydia Mihalik, director of the Ohio Department of Development who was appointed by Republican Governor Mike DeWine, said on X in response to McCain's post, "I don’t care what political party you belong to or which candidate you support. There are lines we shouldn’t cross, and this is one of them. We can disagree on plenty of things without losing our sense of decency." Failed Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, a Republican, said on X, "I’ve seen enough: Amy Acton has defeated Vivek Ramaswamy, and is elected the next Governor of Ohio." Sherrod Brown, Democratic candidate in Ohio for U.S. Senate and former senator, called the ad "disgusting," adding, "Everyone, including Jon Husted, should be willing to condemn this ad." Husted is the Republican incumbent running against Brown in the race for U.S. Senate. Acton’s campaign also released a new 30-second ad Tuesday featuring her brother, who issued a forceful defense of the Democratic gubernatorial candidate, and accused Ramaswamy of having “contempt for Amy,” adding that “he’s not fit to lead.” Laura Loomer, conservative influencer and ally to President Donald Trump, defended Ramaswamy amid the fierce backlash, saying she stands with him. She also reacted to the prediction market odds showing him sinking: "FAKE NEWS @VivekGRamaswamy is soaring in the polls today after @amyactonoh Amy Acton’s own mother disavowed her as a liar. This is completely fake news." Where Polling Stands Acton has been up in a majority of recent polls against Ramaswamy. Election forecaster The Cook Political Report has the race rated as a toss-up, as does Sabato’s Crystal Ball. An ActiVote poll shows Ramaswamy in the lead with 51.4 percent compared to Acton's 48.6 percent. The poll was conducted from September 27 to October 19 among 400 likely voters and had a margin of error of 4.9 percent. This result falls within the average expected error and is a statistical tie. A Marist poll shows Acton with 50 percent compared to Ramaswamy's 43 percent, 3 percent undecided and another 3 percent saying another party's candidate. The poll surveyed 1,176 respondents from October 15 to October 18 and has a margin of error of 4.5 percent among likely voters. A Bowling Green State University Democracy and Public Policy Network/YouGov survey shows Ramaswamy with 44 percent versus Acton's 50 percent. Libertarian Don Kissick landed 4 percent and 2 percent said someone else. The poll surveyed 1,000 Ohio likely voters from September 29 to October 9 and had a margin of error of 3.95 percent. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: The backlash comes as election forecasters rate the race for the Ohio governor's mansion as a toss-up.

news.text:
ANIUS targets $500 bn bilateral trade with India in three years, says Ambassador Sergio Gor

Mumbai: The United States has set an ambitious target to double its bilateral trade with India to over USD 500 billion within the next three years, up from a record-breaking USD 240 billion, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said.Addressing business leaders and diplomats at the Freedom 250 reception in Mumbai, Ambassador Gor highlighted the deepening economic and strategic partnership between the two nations, noting that President Donald Trump sent him to India with a clear mandate -- "Deliver results. Don't just talk about the future. Make it happen".Also read: Marco Rubio, S Jaishankar discuss energy ties as India-US trade deal nears finalisation"In their recent discussions, President Trump and Prime Minister Modi reaffirmed that commitment," Gor said. "Today, our bilateral trade has shattered records, reaching over $240 billion. We have an ambitious goal. We are laser-focused on driving that number past $500 billion in the next three years."Gor emphasised that the upcoming economic expansion spans critical future-facing sectors, including semiconductors, critical minerals, energy, defence, and superintelligence.Live EventsDescribing the momentum of the alliance, Gor stated that the relationship extends from deep-sea infrastructure to space."The US-India partnership does not move in a flat line; it climbs. It begins in the ocean depths with critical data infrastructure. It rises through our factories, labs, and research hubs, and it extends into deep space through commercial exploration," he said. "That is the trajectory of our alliance, rooted deep in fundamentals, accelerating upward at record speed, and heading straight for the stars."Reflecting on the historical tie between the nations during the Freedom 250 event, Gor added, "What we have seen over the next 250 years has been incredible. What we hope to see over the next 250 years will be even more incredible."Highlighting Mumbai's role as an economic hub for the partnership, Gor pointed out that more than 500 major American companies operate in the city, including technology leaders Google, Meta, and IBM; consumer giants Procter & Gamble and Johnson & Johnson; pharmaceutical companies Pfizer, Abbott, and Merck; and financial institutions Citi, Bank of America, and JPMorgan Chase.Furthermore, American institutional investors represent the largest single block of foreign capital in Indian equities traded on Mumbai's stock exchanges."That is not an accident. That is a massive vote of confidence in India's economic trajectory," Gor remarked. "None of this happened by accident, and none of it was built overnight."Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has characterised the strategic alignment between India and the United States as "extraordinary", emphasising that both nations have an opportunity to shape the course of the 21st century through partnership.Addressing the gathering, Rubio observed that while Washington and New Delhi would not see eye to eye on every matter, their shared fundamental interests hold the capacity to influence geopolitics, economics, trade and commerce for decades to come."No two nations on Earth will ever be perfectly aligned on every issue, and there will be times and points of disagreement," Rubio stated."But on the core issues that matter, the core issues that define the national interests of both India and the United States, the alignment between our countries is extraordinary," he added.Rubio underscored that the collaboration carries immense weight given the demographic and economic magnitude of the two powers, characterising India as a country nearing a population of 1.5 billion alongside the United States as the planet's largest economy.He noted that the two countries possess a distinct prospect to contribute towards authoring the history of the 21st century by collaborating closely on matters destined to dictate tomorrow.Furthermore, Rubio expressed the view that the United States ought to maintain more frequent diplomatic engagement with India, which he labelled among Washington's most vital geopolitical partners.In February this year, India and the US announced a framework for an interim trade agreement aimed at improving market access and reducing trade barriers. news.title: 'Deal pretty close': Trump on India-US trade agreement
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 21 (IANS) US President Donald Trump said that India wants to conclude a trade agreement with the United States and indicated that the two countries were close to reaching a deal, while suggesting that the final arrangement would differ significantly from earlier trade agreements. Speaking to reporters during an Oval Office interaction alongside Vice President JD Vance, Trump responded to a question about whether Washington and New Delhi were approaching an agreement. "They want to make a deal. We're going to make a deal pretty close," Trump said. "Yeah, that's going to be a much different kind of deal than we've made," he added. The remarks came as Secretary of State Marco Rubio was visiting India and holding discussions with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, placing the President's comments against the backdrop of high-level diplomatic engagement between the two countries. Trump did not elaborate on what would make the proposed agreement different from previous arrangements. He also did not specify a date for concluding negotiations or identify the remaining issues preventing a final agreement. The President's comments nevertheless suggested that Washington expected progress in talks that have been closely watched by businesses, exporters and investors in both countries. India and the United States have been negotiating a bilateral trade arrangement aimed at expanding market access and addressing longstanding differences over tariffs, agricultural products, industrial goods and regulatory barriers. Trade negotiations have acquired additional significance under Trump's second administration, which has made tariffs and reciprocal market access central elements of American economic policy. The administration has argued that trading partners must offer American businesses greater access to their markets while reducing barriers affecting US exports. For India, the negotiations carry implications for major export sectors, including pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, textiles, electronics and information technology-related services. American companies have also sought greater opportunities in India's expanding consumer market and manufacturing sectors. The President's latest remarks did not indicate whether negotiators had resolved differences over specific sectors or reached agreement on tariff reductions. Nor did he announce any new investment commitments, market-access concessions or implementation timetable. The comments came during an Oval Office event primarily devoted to the administration's efforts to combat fraud involving federal government programmes. Trump and Vance announced new incentives for individuals reporting suspected misuse of taxpayer funds and discussed the administration's broader economic priorities. During the interaction, Trump also spoke about reducing American trade deficits with major trading partners. He cited Canada, Mexico and the European Union while arguing that his administration's trade policies were changing longstanding commercial relationships. The President said the United States was experiencing strong economic growth and attracting substantial new investment in manufacturing and industrial facilities. He presented the administration's tariff and trade strategy as part of a wider effort to strengthen domestic production and employment. Although Trump did not discuss India's tariffs or trade surplus during the exchange, his remarks about the proposed agreement came within that broader economic context. The President's comments followed months of discussions between officials in Washington and New Delhi over the terms of a bilateral trade arrangement. Both governments have identified trade and investment as important pillars of the relationship, alongside defence cooperation, technology partnerships and energy security. The United States is among India's largest trading partners, with bilateral commerce spanning goods and services. The economic relationship also includes substantial investment flows and commercial partnerships involving technology, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing and financial services.

news.title: Trump warns Zelensky to make deal with Russia
news.text:
Washington, Oct 21 (SocialNews.XYZ) US President Donald Trump warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that delaying a peace agreement with Russia could leave Ukraine in an increasingly difficult position, arguing that Moscow was steadily gaining territory and that Kyiv might no longer be able to secure the terms available earlier in the conflict.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office alongside Vice President JD Vance, Trump said Russia's military advantage and Ukraine's mounting casualties made a negotiated settlement increasingly urgent.

The President also disclosed that he had personally discussed the release of an American prisoner, Stephen Hubbard, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and suggested that there could be developments in the case within days.

Trump's remarks came as his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, prepared to travel to Russia following diplomatic discussions in Oslo aimed at advancing efforts to end the war.

"Russia's a big machine. They just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done," Trump said.

He claimed Russian forces were continuing to capture Ukrainian territory and that the military balance was becoming progressively more difficult for Kyiv.

"They've taken a very large piece of land. And, you know, you can say that Ukraine is doing well or poorly, but the land gets bigger and bigger all the time, week by week," he said.

Trump's description of battlefield developments was not accompanied by independently verified territorial data.

The President argued that Russia's larger population gave it a significant advantage in sustaining a prolonged conflict.

He said both countries had suffered enormous casualties but maintained that Ukraine faced greater demographic constraints.

"Ukraine has to want to settle this war. Zelensky has to want to settle this war. And if he doesn't, I think it's going to be a very bad thing," Trump said.

He argued that Zelensky could have negotiated a more favourable agreement during earlier discussions with Washington.

Referring to a previous Oval Office confrontation involving Zelensky, Trump and Vance, the President said the Ukrainian leader had missed an opportunity to secure better terms.

"Could have made a good deal then. Could have made a much better deal then probably, possibly, that he can make now," Trump said.

The President also criticised the scale of American financial and military assistance to Ukraine, saying Washington had spent hundreds of billions of dollars supporting Kyiv.

He claimed the United States had received little in return, although he acknowledged arrangements involving Ukrainian land and rare-earth resources.

Trump said European governments were also growing tired of the financial burden of supporting Ukraine.

He estimated that Russia and Ukraine had together lost 32,000 people during the previous month, describing most of the casualties as soldiers.

The figure was presented as Trump's assessment and was not independently verified.

The President said the continuing deaths were among his principal reasons for seeking a settlement.

"I thought -- you know, I settled eight wars. I thought that would be the easiest one," he said.

Trump attributed the difficulty of reaching an agreement partly to personal hostility between Putin and Zelensky.

"The hatred between President Putin and President Zelensky is tremendous. I think that's most of the reason they haven't been able to make a deal, actually," he said.

Asked whether the Russian and Ukrainian leaders would have to meet in person to conclude an agreement, Trump said such a meeting was not essential.

"They don't have to be in the same room; I guess I can do it another way," he said.

He did not explain what alternative diplomatic arrangement he envisaged.

In a separate exchange, Trump disclosed that he had raised the case of Stephen Hubbard directly with Putin.

"I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard," Trump said.

"I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him, let's see what happens," he added.

The President declined to confirm whether a prisoner-release agreement was imminent but suggested reporters should revisit the matter within a few days.

"I'd love to get him back. It's time to have Mr. Hubbard back," he said.

The comments indicated that the administration was pursuing the prisoner's release through direct engagement with Moscow, although no agreement or timetable was announced.

news.title: US offers $30,000 for tips exposing fraud
news.text:
Washington, Oct 21 (SocialNews.XYZ) The United States has launched a $25 million whistleblower programme offering rewards of up to $30,000 to people whose information helps federal prosecutors bring criminal fraud charges, as the Trump administration steps up efforts to detect misuse of taxpayer money.

The Justice Department announced the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program (WHIP) on Tuesday, introducing a system under which eligible informants can receive payments much earlier than under traditional federal whistleblower arrangements.

The programme will offer awards ranging from $10,000 to $30,000 for original information leading to criminal charges involving specified categories of fraud.

The Department of the Treasury has committed $25 million to support the initiative, which will be administered by the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said the programme would encourage individuals with knowledge of fraudulent activities to come forward.

"Protecting the American people from fraud remains a top priority of the Department of Justice," Blanche said.

He said the initiative would allow people to help expose wrongdoing while receiving financial rewards more quickly than under existing programmes.

The new system differs from traditional whistleblower arrangements because eligible payments can be made after criminal charges are filed and made public, rather than waiting for a conviction, forfeiture proceedings or the conclusion of appeals.

The department said the earlier payment mechanism was intended to encourage prompt disclosure of information and help investigators identify fraudulent schemes before additional public money was lost.

Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald, who heads the National Fraud Enforcement Division, said the initiative would expand the government's ability to obtain information about criminal wrongdoing.

The department said people submitting information must provide original, specific, truthful and timely evidence that contributes to criminal charges.

Participation must be voluntary, and individuals who actively participated in the fraud generally cannot qualify for rewards.

A whistleblower may become eligible when the information leads prosecutors to obtain and unseal an indictment or criminal complaint.

However, the payment is not automatic. The Justice Department retains discretion to determine whether an individual qualifies and whether an award should be made.

The programme also does not require prosecutors to recover a minimum amount of money before considering an early-stage reward.

This distinguishes it from other federal whistleblower schemes in which payments may depend on financial penalties or forfeited assets.

Individuals who receive an early payment may remain eligible for additional awards under separate government whistleblower programmes if their information subsequently results in substantial financial recoveries.

The initiative follows an October 1 directive from McDonald calling for stronger incentives to encourage people to report credible information about fraud.

The department said the programme had been developed in 19 days and would initially operate as a three-year pilot.

Members of the public can submit information through a federal fraud-reporting portal.

The announcement comes as President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have made the detection of fraud involving federal programmes a priority of the administration.

news.title: 'Go to Trump University or die': The Supreme Court's new radical agenda
news.text:
President Donald Trump's Supreme Court is continuing to listen to the legal reasoning of a man whose educational philosophy boils down to "Go to Trump University or die."

That, at least, is the analysis of lawyer and judicial commentator Elie Mystal based on his Tuesday report for The Nation. Mystal described the argument of the new conservatives taking this case to the Supreme Court as influenced by Ed Blum, "the functional spokesperson for the entire white and [Asian American and Pacific Islander] grievance movement, legal gadfly."

The position boils down to being that "every applicant in the country should take a test and the person who scores 'the best' should get into their first-choice school and so on and so forth, until the person who scores the worst can either go to Trump University or kill themselves."

As he wrote at the beginning of his think piece, Mystal explained that "one might think that mediocre white folks and the minority of AAPI parents who have decided to join forces with them would be happy after their victory over affirmative action in the 2023 case known as Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard. They succeeded in their goal of reinterpreting the 14th Amendment as 'colorblind' — notwithstanding the fact that the 14th Amendment was a direct response to over 200 years of slavery and oppression of Black people in the New World — and with it ushered in a new era of 'white makes right' hiring practices."

Mystal reviewed statistics demonstrating that the 2023 Supreme Court decision has effectively ended affirmative action in this country, but added that "despite victory, the victors are not satisfied and will not be satisfied until Black students are drummed out of the system."

The concern, as articulated by Mystal and others, is that one day the same groups dissatisfied with gutting affirmative action will get their case before the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court will be as convinced by Blum’s "Orwellian" solution "to demand 'mandatory public disclosure' of all of a school’s applicants. 'This would include,' he wrote, 'standardized test scores, GPAs, family income, Pell Grant eligibility, AP coursework and other metrics, broken down by race and ethnicity.'"

Mystal asked readers, "Can you imagine applying to a school and, as a result, watching your family’s personal income become a matter of public record? Can you imagine having to share whether or not you are eligible for a Pell Grant with the entire world? Can you imagine having to do all of this because some guy like Ed Blum doesn’t think you belong in school? In three years, Blum has gone from 'universities shouldn’t consider race' to 'universities should make public personal information, broken down by race and ethnicity, for my edification.'"

He concluded, "The goal isn’t just to keep Black and Latino kids out of schools; it’s to discourage them and their parents from even applying."

Mystal is not without cause to be alarmed that the right-wing Supreme Court could once again side with Blum's reasoning on affirmative action issues. In addition to doing so in 2023, they have overturned precedent on a number of other key issues. In July they overturned a precedent more than nine decades ago to effectively empower Trump to fire whoever he wants in the executive branch; they have also helped him construct an illegal White House ballroom, citing a technicality; and gutting the Voting Rights Act to make it easier to disempower non-white votes.

news.title: Americans who moved to Europe after Trump win now say they regret leaving
news.text: Liberal Americans who fled to Europe after President Donald Trump's re-election shared how the grass is not always greener on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean. Wired Magazine released an article Thursday headlined "They Fled Trump’s America. Now They Regret It," speaking directly to those who sought "political refuge in the wake of Trump’s second term," but have since voiced frustration with Europe’s lower quality of life, the rise of right-wing politics in those countries, and a newfound appreciation for the cultural norms and niceties of American life. One account, from a woman nicknamed "Annie," said she was sold the idea of an idyllic U.K. life on social media, "But the reality of life in the U.K. was dramatically different to what she’d imagined." "There are huge misconceptions about access to quality healthcare, standard of living… the quality of life is significantly lower than in the U.S.," she told the magazine, citing challenges ranging from their healthcare system to a significantly lower disposable income. "Things in the U.K. that are considered luxury items are very common" in America, like a dishwasher and dryer, she told Wired. FRENCH AI CEO WARNS AMERICANS AGAINST VOTING DEMOCRAT, SAYING 'YOU DON'T WANT TO BE FRANCE' Annie told the outlet that despite believing she'd have free healthcare under the NHS, she now pays "huge amounts of taxes and an immigration surcharge" to access the national healthcare services. "So no, the health care is not free here," she said. Annie was also surprised by the amount of anti-American hostility she experienced and cultural differences in the workplace. "I found it particularly surprising how people feel so comfortable mocking my accent and culture, even in a workplace environment," she said. "The U.K. is very much a place of ‘it is what it is,’ but as Americans we are taught to always improve and strive for better things." "I thought that ‘British politeness’ existed as it does in movies," Annie added, "but unfortunately, the reality is that present-day British culture is very individualistic, as well as without the sense of charity and helpfulness that many parts of American culture value." WORLD CUP SOCCER FANS ARE DISCOVERING AMERICA’S GREATNESS. IT’S TIME AMERICANS DID, TOO Sarah Wood González, a journalist and consultant, made similar comments about learning to appreciate the American mindset and work culture once she was in a different environment. "Something I had taken for granted is the American outgoingness and default to action, where the question is ‘how can we collaborate?’" she said. "Generally speaking, I also found that the American work style, for better or for worse, moves much faster and can get to a yes or no in less time." "Finding work was so hard, and the endless bureaucracy had grown worse since I’d left," Josh, who moved to Germany, told Wired. "I missed the friendlier people, freedom of speech, and ease of daily life" in the United States, he said. He added of German daily life, "If you aren’t born and raised there, and don’t look German, you’ll never be fully accepted." Josh told the magazine he moved back to the U.S. recently and is much happier. He admitted he may have "overreacted" by fleeing to Europe. Many Americans who shared their regrets on social media were berated by fellow liberals for wanting to move back to "evil" America, the article also said. "These posts are usually met with a huge amount of backlash. Commenters are quick to imply that the poster must be right-wing and privileged, in for a nasty shock if they did return home," Wired Magazine summarized. "Ironically, many times, they parrot the right-wing notion that they probably aren’t trying hard enough to assimilate into their new country. When one person recently said they badly missed their community of friends in a 'blue city in a blue state' and were considering moving back, the majority of top comments agreed the user was 'insane.'" Daniel Di Martino, a Manhattan Institute fellow and economist who was born in Venezuela, spoke to Fox News Digital about how some misguided Americans tend to have unrealistic notions about European life. "Things aren’t always great in Europe, but Europe is not one thing. Living in Greece, making the average salary of a Greek person, would be considered near poverty level in America. Living in Denmark, like an average Dane, is definitely fine, but they still earn much less than the average American," he said. "Some aspects of quality of life in European countries are definitely better: Lower crime, better food. But on the basic reality of how much someone earns, Americans would be worse off moving to Europe." He concluded, "The reason for this is simple: It is very hard to fire workers, so getting a job in the first place is difficult. And in most European countries other than Switzerland and the Baltics, taxes are very high for low and middle-income workers to pay for so-called universal healthcare and pensions for a larger elderly population." "American liberals want to import European socialist ideas and wave after wave of third world immigrants into the U.S., but it turns out that in real life, socialism and mass immigration produce countries that are poorer, less productive, and less enjoyable to call home," he said. "American liberals who moved to Europe are experiencing that firsthand. Every American voter who thinks they want single-payer healthcare should have to spend a few months on an NHS waitlist or look for housing in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin: the European malaise is a real wake-up call."
news.summary: American expats who fled Trump's America now voice frustration with Europe's lower quality of life, bureaucracy, and hostility toward American culture.
news.author: Alexander Hall
